## 4. Measurement results

## 1. Measurement Results

### 1.1 Purpose and Scope

This section records the measurements taken at Valsangone Componenti S.p.A. between 14 October and 14 November 2025 on BR-310 roof rail brackets and on the EN AW-6082 T6 extrusions from which they are machined. The extrusions are supplied by Meccanica Chisone S.r.l. The defect under investigation is a short crack that starts at the edge of one of the four fastening holes (nominal diameter 8.50 mm, tolerance +0.09/0 mm) and runs outward in the plane of the flange, usually 1.5 to 4.5 mm long. The aim of the measurements was to find out which measurable characteristics differ between lots with a high crack rate and lots with a low or zero crack rate. Six extrusion lots were included, covering all lots machined since the first reported crack.

Each bar is 6.0 m long and is sawn into billets that yield 40 brackets per bar. Machining is done on two horizontal machining centres, MC-1 and MC-2, with the same tool set and program. The hole sequence is centre drill, twist drill to 8.30 mm, then a reamer to 8.50 mm. Brackets from every lot were run on both machines.

### 1.2 Gauges Used and Measurement Capability

All gauges were within their calibration interval when used. A gauge repeatability and reproducibility study was run on the hole-diameter and roughness measurements before the lot comparison, using 10 parts, 3 operators and 3 repeats.

| Characteristic | Gauge | Resolution | Gauge R&R (% of tolerance) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hole diameter | Air gauge with 8.50 mm setting ring pair | 0.001 mm | 9.4 |
| Hole position | Coordinate measuring machine (CMM-2) | 0.002 mm | 6.1 |
| Surface roughness Ra in hole | Stylus profilometer, 0.8 mm cut-off | 0.01 µm | 12.8 |
| Burr height at hole exit | Optical measuring microscope, 30x | 0.005 mm | 14.6 |
| Hardness | Brinell tester, 2.5 mm ball, 62.5 kgf | 1 HBW | 7.9 |
| Electrical conductivity | Eddy-current conductivity meter, 60 kHz | 0.1 MS/m | 4.2 |
| Flange thickness | Digital micrometer | 0.001 mm | 5.5 |
| Crack detection | Fluorescent penetrant line plus 10x visual check | not applicable | see 1.7 |

The burr-height result of 14.6 % is acceptable for comparison between lots but not for tight acceptance decisions, and the readings in 1.4 should be read with that in mind.

### 1.7 Detection Capability and Observations

A blind test with 40 brackets (14 with known cracks, 26 without) was run to check the penetrant line. Three inspectors each classified all 40 parts. Detection of cracks longer than 1.5 mm was 100 %, of cracks between 0.8 and 1.5 mm was 79 %, and there were 2 false calls out of 78 classifications on good parts. The 10x visual check in the machining cell detected only 57 % of the cracks longer than 1.5 mm, so the crack rates in 1.3 describe penetrant results and not cell inspection results.

The main observations from the measurements are these:

1. Crack rate varies by a factor of more than 20 between lots, while hole diameter, position and surface roughness do not.
2. Hardness, conductivity, Mn content and elongation separate the lots in the same order as the crack rate.
3. Machine MC-1 shows about twice the crack count of MC-2 across all lots, but the difference narrows to a ratio of 1.3 in the worst lots.
4. Cracks occur preferentially at the holes nearest the extrusion surface.

## 5. D4 Ishikawa analysis

## 2. D4 Ishikawa Analysis

### 2.1 Approach

The cross-functional team met on 3 November 2025 and again on 10 November 2025. The team consisted of the quality engineer (chair), a machining process engineer, a toolroom supervisor, a metrology technician, a production shift leader, a purchasing representative and, by video link, a materials engineer from Meccanica Chisone S.r.l. The effect analysed was: "Cracks of 1.5 to 4.5 mm at the edge of fastening holes on BR-310 brackets, detected after machining, at a sampled rate of 3.9 % overall and up to 11.0 % in single lots."

Each of the six classic branches was brainstormed first without reference to data. Every candidate cause was then screened against the measurements in the previous section and given one of three ratings: unlikely (data contradicts it), possible (data neither supports nor contradicts it), or likely (data supports it). The ratings below are working judgements at the time of writing and are tied to the evidence cited.

### 2.2 Man

The team considered operator influence on loading, clamping and tool change. Three points were examined.

First, clamping force. Brackets are held by two hydraulic clamps. Operators set the hydraulic pressure at the start of each shift, with a nominal value of 55 bar. Spot readings across six shifts showed 52 to 61 bar. Over-clamping could add bending stress near the holes, but the crack position (holes 3 and 4) does not match the clamp positions, which are close to holes 1 and 2.

Second, tool change practice. Operators change the reamer on a count of 600 parts, with a tolerance that in practice allows changes between 560 and 720 parts. Records for L-4519 and L-4520 show the same range as for other lots.

Third, shift distribution. Of the 47 cracked parts, 18 came from the first shift, 16 from the second and 13 from the third, close to the share of production per shift (38 %, 34 % and 28 %). No shift effect was found.

Rating: unlikely as the primary cause. Clamping stays on the list as a possible minor contributor.

### 2.3 Machine

The two machining centres have different spindle ages: MC-1 has 21,400 spindle hours and MC-2 has 9,700. Machine-related candidates were spindle runout, coolant delivery through the tool, and axis behaviour during peck drilling.

Spindle runout measured at the tool tip was 6 µm on MC-1 and 3 µm on MC-2 with a test bar. A runout of 6 µm is within the machine limit of 8 µm but could give uneven reamer loading. This fits the observation that MC-1 shows more cracks than MC-2 in good lots. The effect does not explain why both machines produce high crack rates on L-4519 and L-4520.

Through-tool coolant pressure was 24 bar on MC-1 and 31 bar on MC-2, against a set point of 30 bar. The lower pressure on MC-1 was traced to a partly blocked filter cartridge. Lower coolant pressure may raise cutting temperature at the hole wall, and this is a second reason that MC-1 might be less favourable than MC-2.

Rating: possible, as a contributor that raises crack incidence on MC-1. Not likely as the cause of the large lot-to-lot differences.

### 2.4 Method

The machining method was reviewed step by step. The twist drill step removes 8.30 mm diameter in a single peck cycle at 4,200 rpm and a feed of 0.22 mm per revolution. The reamer takes 0.20 mm on diameter at 1,800 rpm and a feed of 0.35 mm per revolution. The program has not been changed since the start of series production 14 months ago.

Two method weaknesses were identified. The hole is not deburred as a separate operation: the exit burr is removed by a nylon brush in a later station, which leaves a small edge radius of 0.05 to 0.10 mm, a possible local stress raiser. Also, the drilling cycle uses a full-depth peck with no chip break on the last 3 mm, which gave long chips and occasional chip wrapping on the drill (reported by operators on about 1 part in 300).

The sawing and billet preparation method was also noted. Billets are cut with a coolant-flooded saw and stacked on a pallet; no marking of the extrusion surface orientation is applied, so the position of the hole relative to the original outer surface is not controlled. This is consistent with the preferential cracking at holes 3 and 4 but needs confirmation.

Rating: possible. Burr condition and surface orientation are likely contributors only if the material is sensitive to them, since the method was identical for all lots.

### 2.5 Material

This branch received the most attention because of the lot-to-lot pattern. Candidate causes were composition, heat treatment condition, grain structure and extrusion surface condition.

Composition: Mn in L-4519 and L-4520 is 0.46 to 0.47 wt % against 0.62 to 0.63 wt % in the best lots. A lower Mn level reduces the dispersoids that restrain recrystallisation during extrusion and solution treatment, which can lead to a coarse-grained layer near the extrusion surface.

Heat treatment condition: the hardness of 104 to 105 HBW and conductivity of 27.0 to 27.2 MS/m in the worst lots are consistent with a higher degree of precipitation strengthening, for example from a faster quench or a different ageing time. Elongation of 9.2 to 9.6 % is lower than in other lots. A harder, less ductile condition is less tolerant of local cutting stress.

Surface and grain structure: supplier data show a different press line and a different die for the 6 October deliveries compared with earlier lots, according to the supplier representative. This has not yet been confirmed by documents.

Rating: likely. The material evidence has the strongest correlation with crack rate.

### 2.6 Measurement

The measurement branch asked whether the apparent differences between lots could come from the way cracks are found. The penetrant line detects 100 % of cracks over 1.5 mm and 79 % between 0.8 and 1.5 mm. The cell visual check finds 57 % of cracks over 1.5 mm, so most cracks are found only at the later station. Detection capability is the same for all lots, so it cannot explain the lot difference, but it explains why cracks escaped to the later stage. Gauge R&R for hole diameter (9.4 %) and roughness (12.8 %) are acceptable, so diameter and roughness data can be trusted. The supplier certificate Mn values were about 0.08 wt % higher than the laboratory results for two lots, which means incoming checks based only on certificates would not have flagged the difference.

Rating: unlikely as a cause of cracking; possible as a cause of late detection.

### 2.7 Environment

Candidate environmental factors were shop temperature, coolant concentration and storage of extrusions. Shop temperature during the period was 19 to 27 °C, with the highest readings in October afternoons. Machine thermal growth was compensated in all cases. Coolant concentration was checked weekly by refractometer and stayed between 6.5 % and 8.0 % against a target of 7.0 % ± 1.0 %. Extrusion storage is indoors on racks, with a mean time from delivery to machining of 9 days; L-4519 and L-4520 were machined after 7 and 8 days. No link with crack rate was seen for any of these.

Rating: unlikely.

### 2.8 Summary of Ishikawa Ratings

| Branch | Candidate cause | Evidence | Rating |
|---|---|---|---|
| Man | Clamping pressure spread (52 to 61 bar) | Crack positions do not match clamp positions | Possible (minor) |
| Man | Shift effect | Cracks follow production share | Unlikely |
| Machine | Spindle runout 6 µm on MC-1 | MC-1 shows about 2 times more cracks | Possible |
| Machine | Lower coolant pressure on MC-1 (24 bar) | Blocked filter found | Possible |
| Method | Exit burr removed by brush only | Same in all lots | Possible |
| Method | No control of billet surface orientation | Holes 3 and 4 favoured | Possible |
| Material | Lower Mn in two lots | 0.46 to 0.47 vs 0.62 wt % | Likely |
| Material | Higher hardness, lower elongation | 104 to 105 HBW, 9.2 to 9.6 % | Likely |
| Measurement | Cell visual check detection 57 % | Blind test | Possible (late detection) |
| Environment | Temperature, coolant, storage | No correlation | Unlikely |

## 6. D4 Five-why analysis and verification tests

## 3. D4 Five-Why Analysis and Verification Tests

### 3.1 Approach

The Ishikawa ratings in the previous section produced three chains worth following: a material chain, a machining chain, and a detection chain. Each chain was written as a five-why sequence, and each answer was tied to a test or measurement. Where no test has yet been done, the answer is marked as an assumption. The laboratory work was done by the Valsangone metallurgical laboratory, with additional tests at Laboratorio Prove Materiali Orba.

### 3.2 Chain A: Material

| Step | Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Why 1 | Why do the brackets crack at the hole edge? | Fatigue-like or brittle initiation occurs at the hole wall where the reamed surface meets a coarse-grained zone | Fractography, 3.7 |
| Why 2 | Why is the hole wall in a coarse-grained zone? | The extrusion in lots L-4519 and L-4520 has a peripheral coarse-grain layer 1.1 to 1.4 mm deep, against 0.2 to 0.4 mm in the best lots | Metallography, 3.6 |
| Why 3 | Why is the layer deeper in these lots? | Recrystallisation was less restrained during extrusion and solution treatment | Lower Mn (0.46 to 0.47 wt %) and a different press line reported by supplier |
| Why 4 | Why was recrystallisation less restrained? | Mn dispersoid content was lower, and the billet temperature or extrusion speed may have differed | Composition confirmed; process data from supplier not yet received |
| Why 5 | Why was this not detected before delivery? | The supplier certificate Mn value was about 0.08 wt % above the laboratory value, and no grain structure check is part of delivery inspection | Comparison in 1.6; assumption on the supplier check plan |

The chain is supported up to Why 3 by data we hold. Why 4 and Why 5 depend on information from the supplier that is still being collected.

### 3.3 Chain B: Machining

| Step | Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Why 1 | Why does MC-1 give more cracks than MC-2? | Higher cutting temperature and uneven reamer loading at the hole wall | Assumption, partly supported by runout and coolant pressure data |
| Why 2 | Why higher temperature on MC-1? | Coolant pressure of 24 bar instead of 30 bar | Pressure readings |
| Why 3 | Why low pressure? | A partly blocked filter cartridge | Found on inspection |
| Why 4 | Why was it not noticed? | Pressure is not logged and there is no low-pressure alarm below 20 bar | Machine configuration reviewed |
| Why 5 | Why is there no tighter alarm? | The alarm level was set for tool protection, not for process quality | Assumption |

This chain explains a machine difference but not a lot difference, and is therefore treated as a contributing path only.

### 3.4 Chain C: Detection

| Step | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| Why 1 | Why did cracked brackets reach the penetrant line? | The cell visual check detects only 57 % of cracks over 1.5 mm |
| Why 2 | Why so low? | Cracks are tight and sit at hole edges under the brush-finished burr |
| Why 3 | Why is the cell check visual? | It was set up when no cracks had been seen in the product |
| Why 4 | Why was it not reviewed? | No crack events had been recorded in 14 months of production |
| Why 5 | Why was there no early signal? | Incoming material was judged mainly by the certificate |

### 3.5 Verification Tests Overview

| Test | Samples | Purpose | Result in brief |
|---|---|---|---|
| Macro and micro examination of hole cross sections | 6 brackets per lot, 36 total | Grain size and depth of coarse layer | Deep coarse layer in L-4519 and L-4520 |
| Fractography by scanning electron microscope | 8 cracked brackets | Initiation site and mode | Initiation at hole wall in coarse grain |
| Residual stress at hole wall (X-ray method) | 3 brackets per lot, lots L-4472, L-4520 | Machining-induced stress | Tensile stress higher in L-4520 |
| Hole-making trial | 120 brackets, L-4520 bars | Effect of coolant pressure and burr treatment | Cracks reduced but not eliminated |
| Heat treatment re-test | 6 brackets per lot, L-4519, L-4520 | Whether re-ageing changes cracking | Under way for one condition |

### 3.6 Metallography

Cross sections were cut through hole 3 of six brackets per lot, mounted, polished and etched to show grain structure. The depth of the coarse recrystallised layer, measured from the extrusion outer surface, was recorded at four points per section.

| Lot | Coarse layer depth mean (mm) | Maximum (mm) | Grain size in core (µm) | Grain size in layer (µm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L-4471 | 0.28 | 0.41 | 55 | 190 |
| L-4472 | 0.22 | 0.35 | 52 | 175 |
| L-4498 | 0.35 | 0.52 | 58 | 210 |
| L-4519 | 1.12 | 1.46 | 60 | 520 |
| L-4520 | 1.36 | 1.71 | 62 | 560 |
| L-4533 | 0.64 | 0.88 | 59 | 340 |

In the worst lots the hole wall of holes 3 and 4 lies within the coarse layer for most of its length, since those holes are 0.9 to 1.5 mm from the outer surface. In L-4471 and L-4472, the layer is thinner than that distance and the hole wall is mostly in fine core grain. Grain size in the core is similar in all lots, so the difference is confined to the surface layer.

### 3.7 Fractography

Eight cracked brackets (five from L-4520, two from L-4519, one from L-4533) were opened by bending after cooling in liquid nitrogen vapour and examined in the scanning electron microscope. In seven of the eight, the crack started at the hole wall within 0.2 mm of the reamed surface and grew along grain boundaries and through large grains, with flat facets of 300 to 600 µm. One part from L-4533 showed a start at a burr fold at the hole exit, with finer grain at the fracture. Fatigue striations were not found, and the crack face had features of overload and some intergranular separation. No inclusions or porosity larger than 20 µm were found at the initiation sites. The dominant mode is therefore cracking in coarse grain under residual or assembly-related stress, not fatigue from service.

### 3.8 Residual Stress and Hole-Making Trial

Residual stress at the hole wall was measured on brackets from L-4472 and L-4520 at three positions per hole.

| Lot | Hole | Mean tangential stress (MPa) | Range (MPa) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L-4472 | Hole 1 | +42 | +30 to +58 |
| L-4472 | Hole 3 | +51 | +38 to +66 |
| L-4520 | Hole 1 | +64 | +45 to +80 |
| L-4520 | Hole 3 | +118 | +96 to +141 |

The higher stress in L-4520 at hole 3 is consistent with material that is harder and has a coarse surface layer. A trial on 120 brackets from L-4520 bars varied coolant pressure (24 or 30 bar) and edge treatment (brush only, or brush plus a 0.15 mm chamfer cut), 30 brackets per condition. Cracks found by penetrant were 7 of 30 (24 bar, brush), 5 of 30 (30 bar, brush), 3 of 30 (24 bar, chamfer) and 2 of 30 (30 bar, chamfer). Both factors help, but the best condition still shows 6.7 % cracking, so machining changes alone do not remove the problem on this material.

### 3.9 Interpretation and Open Questions

The tests support a link between the coarse-grain surface layer, higher hardness and lower elongation in lots L-4519 and L-4520 and the cracking. They do not yet explain the following points:

1. L-4533, with a layer of 0.64 mm and a crack rate of 2.5 %, shows that the layer depth alone does not give a simple threshold.
2. The reason for the lower Mn and the higher hardness in the 6 October lots is not established, since supplier process records are still awaited.
3. The heat treatment re-test for L-4519 and L-4520 has results for one ageing condition only, with 1 crack in 6 brackets, which is too few to conclude.
4. The contribution of assembly torque to the stress at the hole is not measured, since all cracks were found before assembly.

## 7. D5 and D6 Candidate corrective actions

## 1. Scope and basis for selecting actions

### 1.1 Problem recap
Cracks have been found at the edge of the fastening holes on the BR-310 roof rail bracket. The bracket is machined at Valsangone Componenti S.p.A. from EN AW-6082 extruded profile supplied by Meccanica Chisone S.r.l. Each bracket has four fastening holes, two of diameter 8.5 mm and two of diameter 6.6 mm. The cracks start at the hole edge and run 0.6 to 2.4 mm into the web. They are visible at 10x magnification and were first found in the final visual check.

### 1.2 Why this section lists candidates and not a single fix
The root cause has not been confirmed. Metallography on nine samples and fractography on six samples point to three contributing factors that may act alone or together. The first is a coarse recrystallised grain layer at the extrusion surface, seen in 5 of 9 samples. The second is a burr and a work-hardened rim at the hole edge, linked to drill wear above 70% of tool life. The third is residual stress from the clamping of the profile during drilling. D5 therefore lists corrective actions against each hypothesis. The trials in D6 are designed so that each one can show whether its hypothesis holds. No action is treated as the confirmed fix until its trial results are in.

### 1.3 Selection criteria
Each candidate is rated on four criteria:

- Expected effect on crack incidence, based on the lab evidence.
- Cycle time impact. The BR-310 cell has a takt of 41 s and can tolerate at most +4 s.
- One-off cost and lead time.
- Risk of moving the problem elsewhere, for example into thread quality or hole position.

## 2. Options considered

### 2.1 Option table

| ID | Hypothesis addressed | Candidate action | Expected effect | Cycle time | One-off cost (EUR) | Lead time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Hole edge condition | Reduce drill tool life limit from 1,800 holes to 1,000 holes | Medium | +0.0 s | 900 (extra tool cost per month) | 1 week |
| A2 | Hole edge condition | Change drill geometry to 135 degree split point with polished flute and 0.15 mm edge radius | Medium to high | +0.0 s | 2,400 | 3 weeks |
| A3 | Hole edge condition | Add a chamfer and deburr step with a spring-loaded combined tool in the same station | High | +3.2 s | 5,800 | 4 weeks |
| A4 | Clamping stress | Lower clamp force from 9 kN to 5 kN and add a third support pad under the web | Medium | +0.0 s | 3,100 | 3 weeks |
| A5 | Clamping stress | Re-sequence operations so the 6.6 mm holes are drilled before the profile is side-clamped | Low to medium | +1.1 s | 1,200 | 2 weeks |
| A6 | Extrusion grain layer | Ask Meccanica Chisone to change billet preheat and press exit speed to cut the recrystallised layer depth | High if hypothesis holds | 0 | Supplier cost | 6 to 8 weeks |
| A7 | Extrusion grain layer | Machine 0.5 mm off the surface around the hole zone (spot face) | High | +5.5 s | 7,400 | 6 weeks |
| A8 | Extrusion grain layer | Introduce incoming macro-etch inspection of grain layer depth, 5 pieces per lot | Detection only | 0 | 2,600 | 2 weeks |
| A9 | General | Replace the cutting fluid concentration control with an inline refractometer, target 7% to 8% | Low | 0 | 1,700 | 2 weeks |

### 2.2 Options set aside
A7 (spot face) exceeds the cycle time limit of +4 s and doubles the tool cost, so it is kept only as a fallback. A5 is kept in the plan but only as a combined trial with A4, since alone it is unlikely to change the stress state enough. A9 does not address any confirmed hypothesis. It is included in the plan as a low-cost hygiene measure and will not be counted as evidence of effectiveness.

## 3. D6 trial plan

### 3.1 Trial design principles
All trials use bars from two supplier lots with different measured grain layer depths. Lot L-A has a layer of 0.10 mm to 0.15 mm. Lot L-B has a layer of 0.30 mm to 0.45 mm. Each trial runs both lots, so that a result can be separated from the material effect. Pieces are checked by 10x visual inspection and by eddy current at the hole edge. A sample of 30 pieces per trial cell is cut for metallography.

### 3.2 Trial schedule and owners

| Trial | Actions tested | Pieces per lot | Total pieces | Start | End | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | A1 plus A2 (drill life and geometry) | 600 | 1,200 | 2025-12-01 | 2025-12-05 | Giulia Ferraresi, Process Engineering |
| T2 | A3 (chamfer and deburr step) | 600 | 1,200 | 2025-12-08 | 2025-12-12 | Giulia Ferraresi, Process Engineering |
| T3 | A4 plus A5 (clamp force, support pad, sequence) | 500 | 1,000 | 2025-12-15 | 2025-12-19 | Matteo Bellandi, Tooling and Fixtures |
| T4 | Baseline (no change), to confirm current incidence | 600 | 1,200 | 2025-11-26 | 2025-11-28 | Paola Zanetti, Quality |
| T5 | A6 supplier process change, material from modified press run | 800 | 800 | 2026-01-19 | 2026-01-23 | Ernesto Rinaldi, Supplier Quality |
| T6 | A7 spot face (fallback only, run if T1 to T3 do not reach target) | 400 | 800 | 2026-01-12 | 2026-01-16 | Giulia Ferraresi, Process Engineering |

The baseline trial T4 runs first so that the incidence comparison uses the same inspection method and the same inspectors. Recent production shows 5.5% of pieces rejected for cracks in sorted stock. The baseline is expected to confirm a value between 4% and 7%.

### 3.3 Acceptance criteria for a trial
A trial is considered to have shown an effect when all of the following hold:

1. Crack incidence is 0 in the trial quantity, and the upper 95% confidence limit is at or below 0.25%. With 1,200 pieces and zero findings the upper limit is about 0.25%, so this is the reason for the quantity in T1 and T2.
2. Hole diameter capability Cpk is at least 1.67 on the 8.5 mm holes and 1.50 on the 6.6 mm holes.
3. Thread or fastener torque test on 50 pieces shows no change in failure torque beyond 5% of baseline.
4. Cycle time remains at or below 45 s.

### 3.4 What happens to the data
Every crack found in a trial is sectioned and its starting point is recorded against the grain layer depth, the drill tool life consumed, and the clamp station used. This allows the team to test the three hypotheses directly. If cracks appear only on lot L-B, the grain layer hypothesis gains weight. If cracks follow tool life regardless of lot, the hole edge hypothesis does.

## 8. D7 Preventive actions and lessons learned

## 1. Purpose of D7

### 1.1 What D7 covers
D5 and D6 deal with the BR-310 bracket. D7 deals with the question of how to stop the same type of failure appearing on this product again and on other products that share the same material, the same hole-making method, or the same supplier. Because the cause is not yet confirmed, the preventive actions below are written for the three working hypotheses: surface grain layer, hole edge condition and clamping stress. They apply whichever hypothesis the trials confirm.

### 1.2 Principle
Every preventive action is tied to a gap in the existing process controls, not to a general wish for improvement. Each gap is named below with the evidence that it existed.

## 2. FMEA updates planned

### 2.1 Gaps found in the process FMEA
The process FMEA for the BR-310 drilling and finishing steps did not list cracking at the hole edge as a failure mode. It listed only "hole out of tolerance" and "burr present". Severity for the new mode is set at 8, because a crack at a fastening hole can reduce joint strength. Occurrence was set to 2 on the old sheet only because no cracks had been reported. Detection relied on a 10x visual check at 1 piece in 20, rated 7.

### 2.2 Planned FMEA changes

| Process step | Failure mode added or changed | Severity | Occurrence (before to planned) | Detection (before to planned) | RPN before | RPN planned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Incoming profile | Surface grain layer deeper than 0.20 mm | 8 | 2 to 4 | 8 to 4 | 128 | 128 |
| Drilling 8.5 mm holes | Hole edge work-hardened rim with micro-cracks | 8 | 2 to 3 | 7 to 3 | 112 | 72 |
| Drilling 6.6 mm holes | Hole edge work-hardened rim with micro-cracks | 8 | 2 to 3 | 7 to 3 | 112 | 72 |
| Clamping | Residual stress from clamp force above 5 kN | 7 | 3 to 2 | 8 to 5 | 168 | 70 |
| Deburr and chamfer | Edge radius below 0.10 mm | 6 | 3 to 2 | 6 to 3 | 108 | 36 |
| Final inspection | Crack missed at 10x visual | 8 | 3 to 2 | 7 to 3 | 168 | 48 |

The occurrence and detection values in the "planned" columns are targets. They will be set to final figures only after the trial data are in. The first row shows an unchanged RPN of 128 because the occurrence rating rises to reflect what has been found, while the new incoming macro-etch check improves detection by the same factor.

### 2.3 Method
The FMEA review will be run by a team of five: Process Engineering, Quality, Tooling, Production and Supplier Quality. Ratings are set from measured data where possible: crack incidence from the trials, Cpk from the capability studies, and detection capability from a gauge study using 40 seeded pieces with cracks of 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mm. Review meetings are planned for 2026-01-14 and 2026-02-04.

The mirror arm fitting has one crack in 60 and a grain layer of 0.37 mm, which is higher than any other line. ## 5. Lessons learned

### 5.1 What we learned so far

1. A failure mode that has never occurred is easy to leave out of the FMEA. Cracking at a hole edge was missing, and this left both prevention and detection weak.
2. A sample check of 1 in 20 at 10x finds a 1% defect rate with only about 64% probability across one shift. It is too weak for a safety-relevant hole edge.
3. Certificates from the supplier did not show grain layer depth, because it was not asked for. We ask for what we measure, and we did not measure it.
4. Tool life was set by dimensional wear, not by hole edge quality. These two limits are not the same.
5. Sorting took much longer than planned because the first sorting method, visual only, had a poor detection rate and was repeated with eddy current.

### 5.2 Actions arising from the lessons

## 6. Observations

### 6.1 What drives the cost
Scrap and sorting together make up 60.4% of the incurred cost (EUR 43,254.80). Sorting would have been about 25% lower if eddy current had been used from the first day, because the visual-only method needed rework of 3,100 pieces.

### 6.2 Costs not included
The table does not include lost output on the cell during trials, management time beyond the engineering hours stated, or any effect on the long-term pricing with Meccanica Chisone. These items will be reviewed once the trials are finished, and the cost table will be updated with actual figures for trials and tooling.

title: 8D-26-009 Porosity in HB-620 mount bores, Fonderia Dora
text:
# 8D-26-009 Porosity in HB-620 mount bores, Fonderia Dora

## 1. D0 Symptom and emergency response

## 0.1 Purpose of this section

This section records how the porosity in the mount bores of the HB-620 gearbox mount housing was first noticed at Valsangone Componenti S.p.A., who was told and when, and what was done in the first 72 hours. The housings are die cast in AlSi9Cu3 by Fonderia Dora and machined at the Valsangone plant in Bergamo. The times below are written as hours after first notice (T+0). The clock time of first notice is given once in 0.3.

## 0.2 Part and process background

The HB-620 housing is a gearbox mount housing with two mount bores, called bore A (nominal 42.000 mm, H7) and bore B (nominal 28.000 mm, H7). Both bores are finish-bored on machining line 3 in one clamping. A steel bushing is pressed into each bore at the final assembly cell. The bore walls carry the bushing press fit and the torque reaction of the gearbox, so the drawing limits subsurface and surface pores in these two bores more tightly than in the rest of the casting.

Key process data at the time of notice:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Material | AlSi9Cu3 die cast |
| Casting weight (raw) | 2.84 kg |
| Finished weight | 2.61 kg |
| Machining stock in bores | 0.8 mm per side (bore A), 0.7 mm per side (bore B) |
| Weekly demand | approx. 1,150 pieces |
| Casting supplier cell | Fonderia Dora, die cast cell 4 (1,600 t machine) |
| Machining line | Valsangone line 3, cells M3 and M4 |
| Bore acceptance limit | no single pore above 0.5 mm on the bore wall; no more than 3 pores between 0.3 and 0.5 mm per bore |

## 0.3 First notice

The first notice came on Monday 9 March 2026 at 06:40 (T+0) from the first-shift operator on machining line 3, Nadia Ferraro. After finish boring of bore A on a housing from the third pallet of a delivery, she saw dark pits in the bore wall during her routine visual check under the cell lamp. She stopped the cell, kept the part, and called the shift leader.

Within the first 20 minutes the shift leader, Matteo Cattaneo, took the next 40 consecutive housings from the same pallet and had them checked at the cell with the handheld bore camera. The result was:

| Check at T+0 to T+0:50 | Result |
|---|---|
| Housings checked with bore camera | 40 |
| Housings with pores above the limit in bore A | 9 |
| Housings with pores above the limit in bore B | 4 |
| Housings with pores in both bores | 3 |
| Housings with no finding | 30 |
| Reject rate in this sample | 25.0 % (10 of 40 housings had at least one finding) |

The normal reject rate for this defect on the line over the previous 26 weeks was 0.4 %, so the sample was roughly 60 times higher than usual.

## 0.4 Description of the symptom

The pits were round to irregular, black inside, and between 0.4 mm and 1.8 mm across. On several parts they sat in a line along the parting plane side of bore A. In the worst housing, six pits were counted in one bore, the largest 1.8 mm wide and about 1.2 mm deep. A pit this deep reaches past the finish-bore depth and would leave a void under the bushing seat.

Two observations shaped the first thinking:

- The pits were not visible on the raw casting. They opened only after roughing and finish boring removed the 0.7 to 0.8 mm skin. This points to subsurface gas or shrinkage porosity rather than a surface defect.
- The affected housings carried the same casting date wheel marks, covering production on 4 and 5 March 2026.

## 4. Measurement results

This section records the measurements taken on HB-620 gearbox mount housings die cast in AlSi9Cu3 by Fonderia Dora and machined at Valsangone Componenti S.p.A. The defect under investigation is gas and shrinkage porosity exposed in the two mount bores (bore A and bore B, both finished to Ø42 H7) after finish boring. All measurements were taken between 2026-09-02 and 2026-11-06.

**1.1 Acceptance criteria used for evaluation**

The machined bore surface is evaluated against the following limits from the housing specification. The limits are applied per bore.

| Characteristic | Limit | Applied zone |
|---|---|---|
| Single pore diameter on machined bore surface | ≤ 0.8 mm | Full bore length (38 mm) |
| Number of pores ≥ 0.3 mm | ≤ 3 per bore | Full bore length |
| Pores in the 6 mm sealing land at the open end | none ≥ 0.3 mm | Sealing land |
| Distance between two pores ≥ 0.5 mm | ≥ 5 mm | Full bore length |
| Internal porosity by X-ray around bore (wall 7 to 11 mm) | Grade 2 or better on the plant's 1 to 5 reference scale | 3 mm radial band around bore |
| Pressure decay leak rate, 2.0 bar, 15 s test | ≤ 25 Pa in 15 s | Complete housing |

**1.2 Gauges and inspection equipment**

All gauges were within calibration at the time of use. Resolution is stated where it affects the ability to see the defect.

| ID | Equipment | Range / resolution | Used for | Calibration due |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MQ-114 | Coordinate measuring machine, bridge type | 0.9 µm length accuracy | Bore diameter, roundness, position | 2027-02-28 |
| MQ-131 | Videoscope with Ø6 mm rigid borescope and ring light | 12 µm per pixel at 40 mm working distance | Pore count and pore diameter in bores | 2027-01-15 |
| MQ-072 | Digital measuring microscope, 50x | 2 µm | Pore diameter confirmation | 2026-12-10 |
| MQ-205 | Pressure decay leak tester | 0 to 6 bar, 1 Pa | Leak rate | 2027-03-31 |
| MQ-088 | Real-time X-ray cabinet, 160 kV | 0.1 mm detail recognition | Internal porosity grade | 2027-05-20 |
| MQ-240 | Precision balance with immersion kit | 0.001 g | Density index of sectioned samples | 2027-01-31 |
| MQ-019 | Plug gauge pair Ø42 H7 go / no-go | 0.025 mm tolerance | Line check of bore size | 2027-04-12 |
| MQ-156 | Infrared thermometer | ±1.5 °C | Housing temperature at ejection (supplier visit) | 2026-12-22 |

**1.3 Sampling plan per lot**

Sample size was set by lot size so that a true nonconforming rate of 10 % would be detected with at least 95 % probability. Parts were drawn at random from at least four different pallets per lot. All sampled parts were finish machined and then inspected in both bores with the videoscope.

| Lot size (pcs) | Sample size | Pallets sampled |
|---|---|---|
| 1,200 | 80 | 4 |
| 1,500 | 125 | 5 |

**1.4 Results per lot**

Six consecutive lots from Fonderia Dora were evaluated. A part counts as nonconforming if either bore violates any criterion in 1.1.

| Lot | Cast date | Lot size | Sample | Nonconforming parts | Rate | Bore A fails | Bore B fails | Leak test fails |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DL-4402 | 2026-08-24 | 1,200 | 80 | 2 | 2.5 % | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| DL-4418 | 2026-08-31 | 1,200 | 80 | 3 | 3.8 % | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| DL-4437 | 2026-09-14 | 1,500 | 125 | 11 | 8.8 % | 3 | 8 | 2 |
| DL-4451 | 2026-09-28 | 1,500 | 125 | 17 | 13.6 % | 4 | 13 | 5 |
| DL-4466 | 2026-10-06 | 1,200 | 80 | 12 | 15.0 % | 3 | 9 | 4 |
| DL-4479 | 2026-10-19 | 1,200 | 80 | 5 | 6.3 % | 1 | 4 | 1 |
| **Total** | | **7,800** | **570** | **50** | **8.8 %** | **13** | **37** | **12** |

The first two lots show a rate that is close to the long-term background of about 2 to 3 %. The rate rises sharply from lot DL-4437 and peaks in DL-4466. Bore B accounts for 37 of the 50 nonconforming parts, or 74 %, which is the first strong pointer to a location-specific cause.

**1.5 Pore size distribution**

For the 50 nonconforming parts, every pore of 0.3 mm or larger was measured with MQ-072 after being located with MQ-131. The table shows the distribution of the 188 pores recorded.

| Pore diameter class | Bore A | Bore B | Total | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 to 0.5 mm | 21 | 58 | 79 | 42 % |
| 0.5 to 0.8 mm | 14 | 47 | 61 | 32 % |
| 0.8 to 1.2 mm | 6 | 31 | 37 | 20 % |
| > 1.2 mm | 1 | 10 | 11 | 6 % |
| **Total** | **42** | **146** | **188** | **100 %** |

The largest single pore was 2.1 mm long and elongated along the bore axis, found in bore B of a part from DL-4466. Elongated, irregular pores with rough walls are typical of shrinkage. Round, smooth pores, which are typical of entrapped gas, made up only about 18 % of the count.

**1.6 Pore location along the bore**

The videoscope readings were assigned to three axial zones of bore B (the open end with the sealing land, the mid-length, and the blind end towards the rib junction). Bore A showed a similar but weaker pattern.

| Axial zone of bore B | Distance from open end | Pores ≥ 0.3 mm | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sealing land | 0 to 6 mm | 19 | 13 % |
| Mid-length | 6 to 26 mm | 41 | 28 % |
| Rib junction | 26 to 38 mm | 86 | 59 % |
| **Total** | | **146** | **100 %** |

More than half of the pores lie in the 12 mm adjacent to the rib junction. The rib is 14 mm thick where it meets the boss, against a nominal wall of 7 mm elsewhere. This is the thickest section on the casting and the last region to solidify.

**1.7 Machining stage results and dimensional checks**

Porosity did not change bore size. Across the 570 sampled parts, bore diameter measured on MQ-114 averaged 42.011 mm with a standard deviation of 0.003 mm, and roundness averaged 4 µm. Dimensionally the process is capable, with Cpk 1.9 on diameter. The problem is therefore a surface and subsurface integrity problem and not a machining accuracy problem.

In the same period, scrap booked at the boring operation for "porosity in bore" was:

| Month | Parts machined | Scrapped for bore porosity | Scrap rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| August 2026 | 2,350 | 58 | 2.5 % |
| September 2026 | 2,780 | 241 | 8.7 % |
| October 2026 | 2,610 | 318 | 12.2 % |

The plant scrap rate is consistent with the sample results and confirms that the sample is representative of what the machining line experiences.

**1.8 X-ray and density results on retained samples**

Twenty parts, ten with bore porosity from DL-4451 and ten conforming parts from DL-4402, were examined by X-ray before machining. The results were graded in the 3 mm band around bore B.

| Group | n | Mean grade | Range | Parts at grade 3 or worse |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DL-4402 conforming | 10 | 1.4 | 1 to 2 | 0 |
| DL-4451 with bore porosity | 10 | 3.6 | 3 to 5 | 10 |

Five parts from each group were sectioned through the boss, and the density index of the 20 mm cube from the boss region was measured with MQ-240. Mean density of DL-4402 boss samples was 2.74 g/cm³ and of DL-4451 boss samples 2.66 g/cm³, a difference of about 2.9 %. The metal outside the boss region showed no difference between the groups (2.75 and 2.74 g/cm³), so the effect is local.

**1.9 Measurement system check**

A gauge study was run on MQ-131 with three appraisers, 20 bores and two repetitions each, scoring pass or fail against 1.1. Agreement between appraisers was 93 %, and agreement with the MQ-072 reference was 95 %. Pore diameter measurements on 30 pores gave a repeatability of 0.04 mm and a reproducibility of 0.06 mm, which is 8 % of the 0.8 mm limit. The system is suitable for the purpose, with a recognised weakness for pores under 0.3 mm, which are not counted.

**1.10 Summary of measurement findings**

- The nonconforming rate rose from about 3 % to a peak of 15 % between 2026-09-14 and 2026-10-06 and then began to fall.
- Bore B is affected about three times as often as bore A.
- Pores are predominantly shrinkage in character and concentrate at the rib junction end of the bore.
- Density loss is local to the boss and not general to the casting.
- The measurement system can resolve the defect with acceptable confidence.

## Record

8D report 8D-26-009. Supplier: Fonderia Dora (SUP-D). Opened 2026-08-20. Status: open.
Problem: porosity grade 4 in the mount bores of HB-620 castings (AlSi9Cu3), three escapes to the
Nordhavn line. Root cause: die temperature control. Approval for HB-620 revoked on 2026-09-15.

## 5. D4 Ishikawa analysis

This section analyses possible causes of porosity in the HB-620 mount bores using the six standard categories: man, machine, method, material, measurement and environment. The analysis combines the measurement data from the previous section with interviews and a two-day visit to Fonderia Dora on 2026-10-22 and 2026-10-23, attended by a Valsangone supplier quality engineer, a process engineer and a die casting specialist from an independent consultancy. Each potential cause was rated on evidence: **confirmed** (data shows it contributed), **possible** (plausible, not yet shown) or **excluded** (data shows it did not contribute).

**2.1 Man**

The casting cell at Fonderia Dora runs three shifts. The nonconforming rate was compared by shift for the 570 sampled parts, using the shift stamp on the pallet tag.

| Shift | Parts sampled | Nonconforming | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early (06:00 to 14:00) | 196 | 17 | 8.7 % |
| Late (14:00 to 22:00) | 188 | 16 | 8.5 % |
| Night (22:00 to 06:00) | 186 | 17 | 9.1 % |

The rates are practically identical, so no shift-specific operator behaviour explains the defect. Training records for the nine operators on the cell were reviewed and all had completed the foundry's die casting operator course. One point was noted: the ladling and spray cycle for this die depends on a manual check of the spray nozzle pattern at each shift start, and the check is recorded only as a tick. Two operators described the squeeze pin water flow indicator as "not easy to read". This is a contributing condition rather than a cause of the change in September. Rating: **excluded as a primary cause**, with the readability point carried into the machine category.

**2.2 Machine**

The HB-620 housing is cast on a 1,100 t cold chamber machine with a two-cavity-equivalent single cavity die. The die has a local squeeze pin in the boss of bore B, intended to apply pressure to the last-solidifying region, and a dedicated cooling circuit to that pin and the boss insert.

The checks at the supplier gave the following values.

| Parameter | Specified | Recorded, DL-4402 | Recorded, DL-4466 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Boss insert cooling flow, bore B | 6.5 l/min ± 0.5 | 6.4 l/min | 4.1 l/min |
| Boss insert cooling flow, bore A | 6.5 l/min ± 0.5 | 6.6 l/min | 6.3 l/min |
| Squeeze pin stroke | 18 mm | 18 mm | 18 mm |
| Squeeze pin delay after fill | 3.5 s | 3.5 s | 3.5 s |
| Intensification pressure | 620 bar | 618 bar | 612 bar |
| Boss insert surface temperature before spray | 180 to 220 °C | 204 °C | 251 °C |

The flow through the bore B insert circuit fell by 37 % between the first and the last of the lots reviewed, and the insert ran about 47 °C hotter. A hotter insert delays solidification of the boss and lengthens the time the squeeze pin has to work against a mushy zone that is partly already feeding-starved. The bore A circuit was unchanged, which fits the 74 % bias towards bore B. When the circuit was opened on 2026-10-23, the channel feeding the bore B insert was found to have a partial deposit layer from water treatment, reducing the effective bore by an estimated 30 %. Rating: **confirmed**.

**2.3 Method**

Three process method items were reviewed.

First, the die spray method. The spray cycle was 4.2 s of lubricant per shot in August. A parameter log shows that on 2026-09-09 the cycle was extended to 5.6 s to reduce soldering on the core pin of bore A. The longer spray further cools the surface but also leaves more residual film in the boss, and the shot-to-shot insert temperature trace is more erratic after the change. The extension was not accompanied by any check on the porosity of the boss. Rating: **possible, contributing**.

Second, the fast shot phase and fill time. Fill time was 38 ms in all lots, and the fast shot velocity was 3.4 m/s within a ±0.1 m/s band. No change. Rating: **excluded**.

Third, the in-process inspection method. The foundry's final inspection checks surface appearance and one X-ray part per lot, at a position that does not cover the bore B boss. The method could not detect the rising porosity. Rating: **confirmed as a detection gap**.

**2.4 Material**

The alloy is AlSi9Cu3 supplied as ingot to the foundry's central furnace and delivered by ladle to the holding furnace of the cell. Three material aspects were tested.

| Aspect | Method | Result, DL-4402 | Result, DL-4466 | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chemical composition (spark spectrometer) | Si, Cu, Fe, Mg, Mn | Si 9.1 %, Cu 2.9 %, Fe 0.8 %, Mg 0.28 %, Mn 0.31 % | Si 9.0 %, Cu 3.0 %, Fe 0.8 %, Mg 0.30 %, Mn 0.30 % | Within specification, no difference |
| Reduced pressure density index | Melt sample before cast | 3.1 % | 6.8 % | Gas content raised in DL-4466 |
| Remelt share in charge | Charge sheets | 38 % | 52 % | Higher return material |
| Oxide film index (K-mold) | Fracture rating | 14 mm | 29 mm | Raised in DL-4466 |

Composition is not the cause. However, the density index of the melt rose from 3.1 % to 6.8 %, and the remelt share in the charge rose from 38 % to 52 % after a change in the supplier's scrap handling. High remelt share raises oxide content and gas pick-up. This is a plausible amplifier because gas that is not removed adds to shrinkage voids, and the share of smooth round pores (18 %) shows some gas contribution. Rating: **possible, contributing**.

**2.5 Measurement**

Two measurement aspects need consideration: whether Valsangone's measurements overstate the defect, and whether the supplier's measurements missed it.

On the Valsangone side, the gauge study in section 1.9 shows 95 % agreement with the reference microscope, and no evidence of bias. An overestimate is excluded: of the 188 pores recorded, 11 were re-examined by a sectioned cut and all were confirmed as true voids, none as tool marks or chips. On the supplier side, the single X-ray part per lot is taken from the first five shots after a die change, when the die is still at thermal equilibrium, so the sample cannot represent the later production with the drifted cooling circuit. The foundry also has no routine check of cooling flow, which is read from an analogue flow meter once per shift and not trended. Rating: **excluded at Valsangone, confirmed at supplier as a detection gap**.

**2.6 Environment**

The factors considered were ambient temperature and humidity in the casting hall, the water supply to the die cooling and the machine hall layout.

| Factor | August | September | October | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hall temperature, mean | 31 °C | 27 °C | 21 °C | Cooler, not worse |
| Relative humidity, mean | 58 % | 63 % | 66 % | Small rise |
| Cooling water inlet temperature | 24 °C | 24 °C | 23 °C | Stable |
| Cooling water hardness | 17 °fH | 22 °fH | 27 °fH | Rising |

Hall temperature and humidity changes are too small to affect the casting. The cooling water hardness is different: it rose from 17 to 27 °fH after a change in the plant's softener regeneration schedule, which is consistent with the deposit found in the bore B insert channel. Rating: **confirmed as an upstream cause of the flow loss**.

**2.7 Summary of the Ishikawa evaluation**

| Category | Cause | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Man | Shift or operator differences | Excluded |
| Machine | Reduced cooling flow to bore B insert, hotter boss | Confirmed |
| Method | Longer die spray cycle from 2026-09-09 | Possible, contributing |
| Method | Final inspection does not cover the boss | Confirmed, detection gap |
| Material | Higher remelt share and melt density index | Possible, contributing |
| Measurement | Valsangone gauges overstating the defect | Excluded |
| Measurement | Supplier X-ray and flow monitoring unable to detect drift | Confirmed, detection gap |
| Environment | Rising water hardness leading to scale in cooling channel | Confirmed |

The causes marked confirmed or possible were carried into the five-why analysis and the verification tests.

## 6. D4 Five-why analysis and verification tests

This section follows the confirmed and possible causes from the Ishikawa evaluation through three five-why chains, and then describes the laboratory tests and trials used to verify each link. Chain 1 deals with the occurrence of porosity, chain 2 with the amplifying factors and chain 3 with the escape of the defect to Valsangone.

**3.1 Five-why chain 1: occurrence of shrinkage porosity at the bore B rib junction**

| Level | Question | Answer | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Problem | Why are there pores in the bore B surface after machining? | Shrinkage voids are exposed by boring | Videoscope, pore shape, section cuts |
| Why 1 | Why do shrinkage voids form at the rib junction? | The 14 mm section solidifies last and is not fed enough | Rib is the thickest section; X-ray grades up to 5 |
| Why 2 | Why is it not fed enough? | The squeeze pin works against a boss that is too hot and has already partly solidified at the surface | Insert surface 251 °C against 180 to 220 °C |
| Why 3 | Why is the boss too hot? | Cooling flow through the bore B insert fell from 6.5 to 4.1 l/min | Flow measurement on the die |
| Why 4 | Why did the flow fall? | A deposit layer reduced the channel cross-section | Channel opened on 2026-10-23, deposit found |
| Why 5 | Why did the deposit form? | Water hardness rose from 17 to 27 °fH and no descaling interval or flow trend monitoring existed for the die circuits | Water analysis, maintenance schedule |

Root cause 1 is therefore the lack of a controlled descaling and flow-monitoring routine for the die cooling circuits, combined with a rise in water hardness.

**3.2 Five-why chain 2: amplifying factors from melt and spray**

| Level | Question | Answer | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Problem | Why was the rate of nonconformity higher in lots DL-4451 and DL-4466 than flow loss alone would predict? | Gas and oxide content in the melt were higher, and the die surface was colder at the surface but hotter in the core of the insert | Density index 6.8 %, K-mold 29 mm |
| Why 1 | Why was gas content higher? | Degassing was less effective | Rotor degassing time was 4 min in the log, against 6 min in the standard |
| Why 2 | Why was degassing shortened? | The remelt share rose to 52 % and the furnace was refilled more frequently, so the cycle was cut to keep the cell supplied | Charge sheets, furnace log |
| Why 3 | Why did the remelt share rise? | Gate and runner return was not reduced when yield on a second die was changed | Material balance |
| Why 4 | Why was this not noticed? | There is no trigger limit for remelt share or density index in the process plan | Process plan review |
| Why 5 | Why is there no trigger? | The process plan was written for a stable year-long run and was never updated when the cell took on a second housing | Document review with foundry quality manager |

In the same chain, the longer spray cycle introduced on 2026-09-09 was found to increase the insert temperature variation by 11 °C peak to peak. This was recorded as a minor contributing factor and is addressed in the trials below.

**3.3 Five-why chain 3: escape of the defect to Valsangone**

| Level | Question | Answer | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Problem | Why did parts with porosity at the bore reach the machining line? | Neither the foundry nor Valsangone inspected the bore region before machining | Control plan review |
| Why 1 | Why did the foundry not detect it? | One X-ray part per lot from the first shots only | X-ray log |
| Why 2 | Why only the first shots? | The sampling position was chosen for die set-up approval and never revised for series production | Interview |
| Why 3 | Why did Valsangone incoming inspection not detect it? | The incoming plan checks dimensions and surface appearance, and the bore is raw cast and not accessible to the gauge | Incoming plan |
| Why 4 | Why was the bore not evaluated in incoming inspection? | Historical porosity rates were below 3 %, and the machining stage screens it | Scrap history, 12 months |
| Why 5 | Why was the rising trend not seen earlier? | Machining scrap was reported monthly and aggregated by cause group, so the porosity increase in September was not separated until October | Reporting format |

**3.4 Verification test 1: metallography of the affected region**

Six sectioned bore B boss samples (three from DL-4402, three from DL-4466) were mounted, polished and etched. Observations were made at 50x and 200x.

| Sample | Lot | Secondary dendrite arm spacing | Largest void (section) | Void character | Area fraction of voids |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | DL-4402 | 21 µm | 0.18 mm | Small, interdendritic | 0.4 % |
| M2 | DL-4402 | 23 µm | 0.22 mm | Small, interdendritic | 0.5 % |
| M3 | DL-4402 | 22 µm | 0.15 mm | Small, interdendritic | 0.3 % |
| M4 | DL-4466 | 39 µm | 1.9 mm | Irregular, shrinkage | 3.1 % |
| M5 | DL-4466 | 42 µm | 1.4 mm | Irregular, shrinkage | 2.6 % |
| M6 | DL-4466 | 37 µm | 2.3 mm | Irregular with oxide film | 3.8 % |

The dendrite arm spacing is nearly doubled in DL-4466, which indicates a markedly slower solidification rate in the boss. This directly supports the finding of a hotter insert. Sample M6 showed oxide films lining the void walls, in line with the melt cleanliness result.

**3.5 Verification test 2: hardness and mechanical effect**

Hardness was measured on the machined face next to bore B, 5 measurements per part, on 10 parts per group.

| Group | Mean hardness (HBW 2.5/62.5) | Standard deviation | Minimum |
|---|---|---|---|
| DL-4402 | 91 | 2.1 | 87 |
| DL-4466, no pore in bore | 89 | 2.6 | 84 |
| DL-4466, with pore in bore | 82 | 4.8 | 73 |

The lower, more scattered hardness near the porous region confirms reduced local density. Two tensile bars taken from the boss region of DL-4466 gave 148 and 139 MPa against 196 and 201 MPa from DL-4402. This reduction matters because the bore carries bolt preload and cyclic load from the gearbox.

**3.6 Verification test 3: cooling circuit correction trial**

To prove the cause, the foundry flushed and descaled the bore B insert circuit on 2026-10-24 and restored flow to 6.5 l/min. Spray cycle and remaining parameters were left unchanged, so that only the flow was varied. Two trial runs of 200 parts each were made, with a separate melt batch in each, and 100 parts of each run were machined and inspected at Valsangone.

| Condition | Insert flow | Insert surface temperature | Parts inspected | Nonconforming | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before descaling (DL-4466 data) | 4.1 l/min | 251 °C | 80 | 12 | 15.0 % |
| After descaling, remelt 52 % | 6.5 l/min | 207 °C | 100 | 5 | 5.0 % |
| After descaling, remelt 35 % and 6 min degassing | 6.5 l/min | 205 °C | 100 | 2 | 2.0 % |

Restoring flow cut the rate from 15.0 % to 5.0 %, which is about two thirds of the problem. Adding the melt measures cut it further to 2.0 %, back in the background range seen in August. This is consistent with chain 1 as the main cause and chain 2 as the amplifier.

**3.7 Verification test 4: spray cycle comparison**

A short trial of 50 parts per condition compared the 5.6 s spray cycle with the earlier 4.2 s cycle, with cooling flow restored and the melt at normal state.

| Spray cycle | Insert temperature variation (peak to peak) | Parts inspected | Nonconforming |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.6 s | 19 °C | 50 | 2 |
| 4.2 s | 8 °C | 50 | 1 |

The difference in nonconforming parts is within sampling noise, so the longer spray cycle is a minor factor on its own and is not a root cause, although it increases temperature scatter.

**3.8 Verification of the detection gap**

The foundry's X-ray plan was replayed against retained X-ray images. A sampling position of one part per lot from the first five shots would have detected porosity grade 3 or worse in the boss in 0 of the 6 lots reviewed. A plan of 3 parts per lot, taken at start, mid and end of run, and including the bore B boss in the field of view, would have detected it in 4 of the 6 lots, including the three highest-rate lots. This confirms that the detection gap in chain 3 is real and that a repositioned X-ray sample would have given earlier warning.

**3.9 Conclusions from the analysis and tests**

- Root cause of occurrence: slow solidification of the bore B boss due to reduced insert cooling flow, caused by scale deposit from harder water and no descaling or flow trend routine.
- Amplifying cause: higher remelt share and shortened degassing, resulting in melt density index of 6.8 %.
- Minor contributing factor: longer spray cycle, with a measurable effect only on temperature variation.
- Root cause of escape: sampling and incoming inspection plans that did not examine the bore region, and monthly aggregated scrap reporting.

These conclusions are the basis for the corrective actions in the later sections of this report.

## 7. D5 and D6 Candidate corrective actions

## 1. D5 and D6 Candidate Corrective Actions

### 1.1 Basis for the action options
The actions below address the two verified cause groups for porosity in the two Ø42 H7 mount bores of the HB-620 gearbox mount housing, die cast in AlSi9Cu3 by Fonderia Dora on its 840 t cold-chamber press. Sectioning and CT scanning of 46 housings showed gas and shrinkage pores of 0.8 to 2.4 mm, clustered 6 to 10 mm below the cast bore surface. This is the region of the 19 mm boss, which is thick compared with the 8 mm nominal wall around it.

The cause groups are:

- **Occurrence cause 1: gas entrapment.** The vacuum valve channel on the die was partly blocked. Measured cavity vacuum was 180 to 260 mbar against a 80 mbar requirement. Spray volume of die lubricant was also high at the boss insert.
- **Occurrence cause 2: localized hot spot.** The boss insert ran 38 °C above the die average. Intensification pressure was applied late, so the last-solidifying zone was not fed.
- **Escape cause:** Fonderia Dora checked only surface appearance and one X-ray piece per shift. Valsangone incoming inspection checked dimensions only, so porosity was found at the machining cell after the bores were finished.

### 1.2 Options considered
Eight options were scored by the 8D team on effectiveness against each cause (1 to 5), cost, lead time and implementation risk. The team also weighed the effect each option has on the established process window.

| ID | Option | Cause addressed | Effectiveness (1–5) | Est. cost (EUR) | Lead time | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Clean and redesign vacuum channel; add vacuum sensor with shot-by-shot interlock | Gas | 5 | 9,800 | 3 weeks | Low |
| B | Reduce lubricant spray volume at boss insert from 1.8 to 1.1 mL per shot | Gas | 3 | 0 | 1 week | Low |
| C | Spot cooling (pulsed jet) in boss insert | Hot spot | 4 | 6,400 | 4 weeks | Medium |
| D | Squeeze pin in boss, 12 mm stroke | Hot spot | 5 | 14,200 | 7 weeks | Medium |
| E | Retune shot profile: earlier intensification, slow-shot 0.22 m/s | Both | 3 | 1,500 | 2 weeks | Medium |
| F | Add boss rib to reduce thickness to 14 mm | Hot spot | 5 | 38,000 | 16 weeks | High |
| G | Switch to semi-solid or low-pressure process | Both | 4 | 210,000 | 9 months | High |
| H | 100% X-ray at Fonderia Dora end of line | Escape | 2 | 31,000 per year | 4 weeks | Low |

Option F changes part geometry and option G changes the process route. Both were set aside because their lead times do not suit the delivery schedule, and because options A, C, D and E are expected to reach the target without them. Option H detects the defect but does not remove it, so it is kept only as an interim barrier.

### 1.3 Selected actions
The team selected a package of five actions, ranked by expected effect:

1. **A1 (option A):** Rebuild the vacuum channel with a larger 6 mm passage and a chill-vent block. Fit a pressure sensor with a shot-by-shot interlock that rejects any shot above 100 mbar at fill end.
2. **A2 (option B):** Cut the spray volume at the boss insert to 1.1 mL per shot and add a 2 s air purge before closing.
3. **A3 (option C):** Install pulsed spot cooling in the boss insert, targeting a 20 °C reduction in local temperature.
4. **A4 (option E):** Retune the shot profile with intensification starting 0.04 s earlier.
5. **A5 (option D):** Squeeze pin, held in reserve. It is built only if trials of A1 to A4 do not meet the criteria in section 1.5. The pin and its insert are ordered at risk because of the 7-week lead time.

Two escape-side actions complete the package:

6. **A6:** Valsangone adds a CT or X-ray sampling plan at incoming inspection for the bore zone: 5 pieces per lot for the first 20 lots, then 3 pieces per lot.
7. **A7:** Fonderia Dora moves bore-zone X-ray from one piece per shift to five pieces per shift, using a defined acceptance image set.

### 1.4 Trial plan
Trials are run at Fonderia Dora with Valsangone engineers present. Each trial uses a single factor change where possible, so the effect can be separated. Pieces are marked by shot number and cavity.

| Trial | Content | Parameters | Sample | Start date | Duration | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Baseline with current settings | Spray 1.8 mL, vacuum as found | 200 shots | 23 Nov 2026 | 1 shift | L. Brambilla (Dora process eng.) |
| T2 | Vacuum channel rebuilt (A1) | Target ≤ 80 mbar | 300 shots | 25 Nov 2026 | 1.5 shifts | L. Brambilla |
| T3 | A1 plus reduced spray (A2) | Spray 1.1 mL, purge 2 s | 300 shots | 27 Nov 2026 | 1.5 shifts | L. Brambilla |
| T4 | A1 + A2 + shot profile (A4) | Intensification −0.04 s | 300 shots | 30 Nov 2026 | 1.5 shifts | M. Ferraro (Valsangone process eng.) |
| T5 | A1 + A2 + A4 + spot cooling (A3) | Boss insert 20 °C lower | 400 shots | 7 Dec 2026 | 2 shifts | M. Ferraro |
| T6 | Confirmation run | Best settings, 3 consecutive lots | 3 × 1,000 pcs | 14 Dec 2026 | 3 days | S. Okafor (Valsangone SQE) |

The cooling hardware for T5 is expected on site on 3 December 2026. If it is late, T5 moves to the first available shift after delivery and T6 moves with it.

### 1.5 Acceptance criteria for the trials
A trial result counts as acceptable only when all the following are met:

- No pore larger than 0.5 mm within 3 mm of the finished bore surface, and no pore larger than 1.0 mm anywhere in the boss, from CT of 30 pieces per trial.
- Porosity area share in the boss section of 1.0% or less on 12 metallographic sections.
- Fill-end vacuum at or below 100 mbar on 100% of shots, with a mean of 80 mbar or less.
- Machined bore scrap at Valsangone of 0.3% or less across the confirmation lots, against 5.1% in the affected deliveries.
- Dimensional check on the bores: Cpk of 1.67 or more on the Ø42 H7 diameter after machining.
- No new defects such as cold shuts or soldering, checked by visual review of 100% of trial pieces.

### 1.6 Owners and dates

| Action | Description | Owner | Support | Planned start | Planned finish |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Vacuum channel rebuild and sensor interlock | L. Brambilla | Dora toolroom | 16 Nov 2026 | 24 Nov 2026 |
| A2 | Spray volume cut and purge | L. Brambilla | Dora operators | 24 Nov 2026 | 26 Nov 2026 |
| A3 | Spot cooling in boss insert | G. Ricci (Dora toolroom) | M. Ferraro | 16 Nov 2026 | 4 Dec 2026 |
| A4 | Shot profile retune | M. Ferraro | L. Brambilla | 30 Nov 2026 | 3 Dec 2026 |
| A5 | Squeeze pin, reserve | G. Ricci | Valsangone tooling | 16 Nov 2026 | 8 Jan 2027 |
| A6 | Valsangone incoming bore-zone sampling | S. Okafor | Incoming inspection | 16 Nov 2026 | 20 Nov 2026 |
| A7 | Dora end-of-line X-ray frequency | D. Moretti (Dora quality) | Dora shift leaders | 16 Nov 2026 | 20 Nov 2026 |

### 1.7 Risks and contingencies
The main risks and the planned responses are:

- **Cooling reduces fill quality.** Colder insert zones can cause cold shuts. Response: run T5 with a ramped cooling rate and review every piece visually.
- **Vacuum sensor false rejects.** A tight interlock may stop the press. Response: set a 3-shot rolling alarm first, then switch to the single-shot limit after 5 days of data.
- **Trial parts mixed with production.** Response: trial pieces carry a paint marker and go into labeled boxes only.
- **Delay of A5 tooling.** The reserve pin is ordered early so the 7-week lead time does not slow a later decision.

### 1.8 D6 verification of effectiveness
After T6, Valsangone keeps a heightened inspection period of 10 production lots. During this period the incoming CT sampling stays at 5 pieces per lot and the machining cell logs every bore rejection by shot number. The planned review is on 11 January 2027. It compares bore scrap rate, vacuum trend, boss-zone CT results and casting soundness against the criteria in section 1.5. Results are presented in the form of a run chart of weekly scrap rate and a capability summary. The review team consists of S. Okafor, M. Ferraro, L. Brambilla and D. Moretti.

## 8. D7 Preventive actions and lessons learned

## 2. D7 Preventive Actions and Lessons Learned

### 2.1 Purpose
This section describes how the findings on HB-620 mount bore porosity are carried into the wider system. The aim is that the same escape path (a thick boss, weak vacuum control, and a surface-only check at the foundry) cannot recur on this part or on similar die cast parts at Valsangone Componenti S.p.A. All dates are planned dates.

### 2.2 Process FMEA updates planned
The process FMEA for HB-620 die casting and machining will be revised after the trials in section 1 give new occurrence data. The ratings use the 1 to 10 scales already in use. Planned changes are listed below.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Vacuum assist | Vacuum channel blocked | 8 / 5 / 7 (280) | 8 / 2 / 3 (48) | Shot-by-shot sensor interlock replaces monthly manual check | L. Brambilla | 18 Dec 2026 |

| F5 | Foundry final inspection | Internal porosity not detected | 8 / 4 / 9 (288) | 8 / 3 / 4 (96) | Five X-ray pieces per shift with defined image set | D. Moretti | 4 Dec 2026 |

The six highest RPN values before the change were F2, F3, F5, F6, F1 and F4. Their combined drop from 1,757 to 486 is the planned estimate, and the team will re-rate it once trial data on actual occurrence exist.

### 2.3 Control plan updates planned
The control plan changes mirror the FMEA changes. Each added control has a defined reaction plan.

| Characteristic | Method | Frequency | Limit | Reaction plan | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fill-end vacuum | Pressure sensor, logged | Every shot | ≤ 100 mbar | Shot rejected and diverted; 3 consecutive rejects stop the press | L. Brambilla |
| Vacuum channel flow | Flow gauge test | Every 2,000 shots | ≥ 90% of reference | Clean channel, quarantine shots since last pass | L. Brambilla |

The sampling frequency at Valsangone drops from 5 to 3 pieces per lot only after 20 consecutive lots meet the limits.

### 2.4 Other lines and parts checked
To find where the same exposure may exist, the team reviewed other die cast parts at Valsangone from Fonderia Dora and from two other foundries. The screening criteria were a boss thicker than 15 mm next to a thin wall, a machined bore through that boss, and vacuum assist in use.

| Part | Supplier | Alloy | Boss thickness | Machined bore through boss | Vacuum sensor in place | Finding | Planned follow-up | Owner | Date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HB-540 mount bracket | Fonderia Dora | AlSi9Cu3 | 17 mm | Yes | No | Same exposure | Same sensor and spray changes | L. Brambilla | 29 Jan 2027 |
| HB-710 cross member housing | Fonderia Dora | AlSi9Cu3 | 21 mm | Yes | No | Same exposure | CT of 30 pieces, then sensor | M. Ferraro | 29 Jan 2027 |
| GC-210 pump cover | Fonderia Dora | AlSi9Cu3 | 11 mm | No | Yes | Not exposed | None | – | – |
| GC-330 bearing housing | Fonderia Lenzi | AlSi10Mg | 16 mm | Yes | Yes | Weak trend: one pore finding in 2025 | CT of 20 pieces | S. Okafor | 18 Dec 2026 |
| SK-118 sensor flange | Pressofusione Tarri | AlSi9Cu3 | 9 mm | No | Yes | Not exposed | None | – | – |
| SK-402 actuator body | Pressofusione Tarri | AlSi9Cu3 | 18 mm | Yes | No | Same exposure | Supplier audit of vacuum control | S. Okafor | 15 Jan 2027 |

Four of the six parts were found to have some exposure. Parts HB-540 and HB-710 share Fonderia Dora's machine, so their review is timed to follow the final HB-620 settings. For the three exposed parts without a vacuum sensor, an interim step is one extra CT piece per lot until the sensor is fitted.

### 2.5 Lessons learned

1. **A dimension-only incoming check cannot catch internal defects.** The pores lay 6 to 10 mm below the cast surface and became visible only when the bores were machined. Valsangone now matches incoming inspection to the failure mode of the part, not only to its drawing dimensions.
2. **Vacuum is a process characteristic, not a maintenance item.** A monthly manual check allowed a partly blocked channel to run for an estimated 5 weeks. Continuous measurement is the lesson, and it is the basis of control F1.
3. **A thick boss needs thermal control.** The 38 °C temperature excess at the boss insert was never measured. Thermocouples at known hot spots are now a standard question in die design reviews.
4. **A change in spray settings is a process change.** The spray volume had been raised from 1.2 to 1.8 mL to reduce soldering and was not rechecked against porosity. Any such change now needs a short CT check on 10 pieces.
5. **Sampling frequency of one piece per shift is too low for this defect.** A pore cluster present in about 5% of shots can be missed for many shifts. The foundry's new frequency is based on that detection probability.
6. **Early containment worked best when it used a quick method.** Borescope checks at 3 minutes per piece were slower than the X-ray station at 40 seconds. Valsangone keeps one X-ray station reserved for containment.

### 2.6 Training and communication
Dora operators and shift leaders will be trained on the new spray and vacuum controls on 26 November 2026, with 14 people expected. Valsangone incoming inspectors and cell operators (9 people) are trained on the CT and X-ray image set on 20 November 2026. A one-page summary of lessons 1 to 6 goes to the Valsangone supplier quality team and the Fonderia Dora plant manager by 18 December 2026. The foundry design review checklist gets two new questions: boss thickness ratio and vacuum monitoring. The design owner is E. Valli, with a planned date of 29 January 2027.
