title: NCR-26-017 CL-115 hardness out of tolerance
text:
# NCR-26-017 CL-115 hardness out of tolerance

## 1. D0 Symptom and emergency response

### 0.1 Summary of the symptom

CL-115 is a stamped and hardened cable clip made from 1.2 mm C67S spring steel strip. Valsangone Componenti S.p.A. buys it from Minuterie Germanasca. At the Valsangone plant, a polymer sleeve is pressed onto each clip in the sleeve-insertion cell, and the clip is then packed into kits of 200 pieces. The drawing requires a hardness of 410 to 450 HV1 after tempering. This corresponds to a clip that bends elastically through its full snap-in travel and returns to shape.

On Tuesday 3 November 2026, operators in the sleeve-insertion cell found that clips were cracking at the bend radius of the retaining tab. This happened when the tab was pressed over the sleeve shoulder. Cracking was audible and visible, and it was not seen on earlier shifts. A bench check that morning measured clips between 485 and 540 HV1. This is 35 to 90 HV1 above the upper limit. A clip this hard has low ductility and may fracture during installation or later in service. For that reason the finding was treated as a risk to the function of delivered parts, not only as a production loss.

### 0.2 First notice

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Date and time of first notice | Tuesday 3 November 2026, 07:40 |
| Detected by | Nadia Zanetti, operator, sleeve-insertion cell, first shift |
| Place | Cell 3, assembly hall B |
| Observation | 11 of the first 60 clips pressed after the 06:00 start cracked at the tab radius. The usual rate is fewer than 1 in 2,000. |
| Clip delivery in use | The fourth of four recent deliveries, received on Monday 2 November 2026 (30,000 pieces) |
| Reported to | Luca Ferrando, production supervisor, at 07:44 |

Zanetti stopped the cell on her own judgment and put the cracked clips in a labelled tray. She did not discard them, which kept the fracture surfaces intact for the laboratory. Ferrando came to the cell within four minutes. He saw that the cracks started on the outer face of the bend, and he ruled out the press setting as the cause by running a set of clips from the previous delivery on the same tooling. Those clips pressed without cracks.

### 0.3 Who was informed and when

The information went out in the order below. The aim was for quality, warehouse and purchasing to hold the same facts before anyone made a decision about stock.

| Time (3 Nov) | Person informed | Role | By whom | Channel | Content |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 07:44 | Luca Ferrando | Production supervisor | N. Zanetti | In person | Cracking at the tab radius, cell stopped |
| 07:58 | Paola Rinaldi | Incoming inspection lead | L. Ferrando | Phone | Request for hardness check on retained clips |
| 08:35 | Marco Ghiotto | Supplier quality engineer | P. Rinaldi | In person | First readings 485 to 540 HV1 |
| 08:50 | Elena Bertarelli | Quality manager | M. Ghiotto | Phone and message | Stock at risk, request to open an NCR |
| 09:10 | Sabrina Oldani | Warehouse coordinator | E. Bertarelli | Phone | Immediate stock freeze on CL-115 |
| 09:25 | Giorgio Tessari | Purchasing | E. Bertarelli | Phone | Supplier contact needed, no new call-offs |
| 10:30 | Stefano Marchesini | Quality manager, Minuterie Germanasca | M. Ghiotto | Phone, then email | Symptom, readings and lot dates |
| 11:15 | Roberto Fenoglio | Customer quality liaison | E. Bertarelli | Phone | Parts from earlier deliveries are possibly affected, shipments in transit |
| 14:00 | Plant manager and operations team | Management | E. Bertarelli | Short meeting | Facts, actions taken, plan for the next 24 hours |

The customer quality liaison was told that part of the delivered quantity might be affected, and that Valsangone did not yet know how much. Valsangone made no estimate of the affected share until the sorting data was available.

### 0.4 First actions in hours

The table below records the first 72 hours as hours after first notice (T+0 is 07:40 on 3 November). It lists what was done and who did it.

| Hours from first notice | Action | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| T+0.0 to T+0.1 | Cell 3 stopped, cracked clips saved in a tray | N. Zanetti |
| T+0.3 | Same tooling checked with clips from the previous delivery, no cracks | L. Ferrando |
| T+0.9 | Bench hardness readings on 12 clips from the fourth delivery | P. Rinaldi |
| T+1.5 | Cell 3 and all CL-115 line-side containers tagged red | L. Ferrando |
| T+1.5 | Quality manager informed, NCR started | M. Ghiotto, E. Bertarelli |
| T+1.9 | Stock freeze on CL-115 in the ERP system and in the warehouse | S. Oldani |
| T+2.8 | Supplier informed by phone | M. Ghiotto |
| T+3.5 | Customer quality liaison informed | E. Bertarelli |
| T+4.5 | 30 clips from the fourth delivery sent to the metallurgical laboratory for a full hardness profile | D. Cossu |
| T+6.3 | Management meeting, containment task assigned | E. Bertarelli |
| T+8 | Shift handover with a written note on cell 3 for the second and third shifts | L. Ferrando |
| T+10 | Laboratory results for 30 clips: mean 512 HV1, minimum 487, maximum 541 | D. Cossu |
| T+14 | Samples from the first three deliveries drawn from retained stock, 30 clips from each | P. Rinaldi |
| T+22 | Hardness results for those three deliveries received (see 0.6) | D. Cossu |
| T+24 | Written report to the supplier with the measurement data and photographs | M. Ghiotto |
| T+30 | Count of all stock locations started, with a list of shipped quantities | S. Oldani |
| T+48 | Supplier phone meeting, supplier asked to check its tempering records | M. Ghiotto, S. Marchesini |
| T+72 | Containment plan prepared for the sorting work described in D3 | E. Bertarelli |

### 0.5 Protective actions in the first shift

#### 0.5.1 Stopping the process

Cell 3 stayed stopped until the laboratory had measured the clips. The two other cells that press sleeves onto CL-115 were checked by their supervisors at 08:20. Cell 1 had last run CL-115 on 29 October, and cell 2 was running a different clip. Only cell 3 held clips from the fourth delivery.

#### 0.5.2 Protecting people

A fractured clip can have a sharp edge, and a clip that breaks under tension can fly off. Ferrando told the cell operators to wear safety glasses and cut-resistant gloves while pressing clips, until the cell was stopped. Zanetti noticed no injuries. The cracked clips were collected with a magnet, not by hand.

#### 0.5.3 Protecting stock

The warehouse freeze blocked the picking of CL-115 in the ERP system, so a clip could not be sent to a line by mistake. The physical red tags on every pallet, bin and kit carton were added because the ERP block does not stop a person who takes parts by hand. Oldani made one walk through the warehouse at 10:00 and one through the hall at 10:40, and found no tags missing.

#### 0.5.4 Protecting the delivered quantity

The first concern was that kits might already have reached the customer. At T+30 hours, Oldani's list showed that 46,000 clips, in five shipments, had left Valsangone since 12 October. The customer quality liaison received the dates and kit quantities of the five shipments on the afternoon of 4 November, so that the customer could check its own receiving stock while Valsangone began its sorting.

### 0.6 Early data

The retained samples gave the following picture. Hardness was measured with a micro-hardness tester at 1 kgf on a ground cross-section at mid-leg.

| Delivery | Date received | Quantity | Clips measured | Mean HV1 | Min HV1 | Max HV1 | Clips out of 410 to 450 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 12 October 2026 | 48,000 | 30 | 438 | 421 | 452 | 2 of 30 |
| 2 | 19 October 2026 | 48,000 | 30 | 447 | 428 | 471 | 8 of 30 |
| 3 | 26 October 2026 | 60,000 | 30 | 493 | 468 | 524 | 30 of 30 |
| 4 | 2 November 2026 | 30,000 | 30 | 512 | 487 | 541 | 30 of 30 |

The hardness rises across the four deliveries. This points to a drift over time at the supplier, and not to a single bad lot. At this point the cause is unknown. A tempering temperature that was too low, a belt speed that was too high, or a change of strip material are all possible. D0 does not choose between them, and the supplier was asked for its records.

The data also shows that the whole quantity could not be released, because even the first two deliveries contained out-of-limit clips. Sampling of 30 pieces cannot show the actual share of bad clips in a delivery of 48,000. For this reason the team decided to sort every piece, and to design the sorting so that it can handle large quantities (see D3).

### 0.7 Open information needs at the end of the emergency phase

- The supplier's tempering furnace records, with temperatures and belt speed, for all four delivery dates.
- The strip coil certificates for the material used in each delivery.
- A reading of the hardness of the supplier's own retained samples.
- A decision on how many clips the plant needs in the next two weeks, so that production planning can use sorted stock or a replacement supply.

These needs were handed to the team formed under D1.

## 2. D1 Team

## D1 Team

### 1.1 Purpose and principle

The team leader is Marco Ghiotto, supplier quality engineer at Valsangone. The sponsor is Elena Bertarelli, quality manager, who gives the team access to people and equipment. She does not take part in daily work.

### 1.2 Team members at Valsangone Componenti S.p.A.

| No. | Name | Position | Role in the team | Main responsibility | Stand-in |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Elena Bertarelli | Quality manager | Sponsor | Resources, escalation, contact with the plant manager | Plant manager's deputy |
| 2 | Marco Ghiotto | Supplier quality engineer | Team leader | Plan, meetings, supplier contact, the file | Anita Maffeis |
| 3 | Paola Rinaldi | Incoming inspection lead | Measurement and sorting lead | Sampling, sorting method, inspectors | Matteo Crivelli |
| 4 | Davide Cossu | Metallurgical laboratory technician | Laboratory analysis | Hardness profiles, micro-sections, fracture surfaces | Valentina Sartori |
| 5 | Luca Ferrando | Production supervisor, assembly hall B | Production representative | Cells 1 to 3, line-side stock, rework labour | Claudio Pernigotti |
| 6 | Sabrina Oldani | Warehouse coordinator | Stock and logistics | Counts, locations, ERP blocks, shipment history | Fabio Dellera |
| 7 | Giorgio Tessari | Purchasing buyer | Commercial contact | Call-offs, replacement supply, supplier commercial terms | Ornella Baggio |
| 8 | Anita Maffeis | Process engineer | Process knowledge | Press and tooling data, clip function requirements | Luca Ferrando |
| 9 | Roberto Fenoglio | Customer quality liaison | Customer contact | Information to the customer and answers to its questions | Elena Bertarelli |
| 10 | Nadia Zanetti | Operator, cell 3 | Shop-floor voice | Description of the first finding, practical advice on sorting | Operator on the second shift |

Ten people from Valsangone are in the team. The operator was included on purpose. She found the problem, and she can say how the cracking looked, which fracture sounds she heard and how the clips felt different when pressed. These details are often missing from reports written later.

### 1.3 Team members at Minuterie Germanasca

Minuterie Germanasca is a stamping and heat treatment company with about 140 employees. Its plant is in the Val Germanasca area, about 95 km from Valsangone. Its quality manager joined the team on 4 November 2026, after the phone call on the previous day and the written report. The other supplier members joined on 5 November.

| No. | Name | Position | Role in the team | Main responsibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11 | Stefano Marchesini | Quality manager | Supplier lead | Access to records and people at the supplier, answers to the team |
| 12 | Ilaria Bonomelli | Heat treatment process engineer | Process expert | Furnace set points, belt speed, temperature profile records |
| 13 | Tommaso Gervasoni | Metallurgist | Material and laboratory | The supplier's own hardness checks, strip certificates |
| 14 | Cesare Pedretti | Production manager | Operations | Stock held at the supplier, capacity for replacement supply |
| 15 | Chiara Bellandi | Key account manager | Commercial contact | Contact with Valsangone purchasing |

The heat treatment engineer and the metallurgist are the two people who can say what happened to the clips in the supplier's process. For this reason the team asked that they be named from the start, and not only the quality manager.

### 1.4 Roles during the work

The table below shows who does what in each phase of the investigation. R means that the person carries out the task, A means that the person is accountable for the result, C means that the person is consulted, and I means that the person is informed.

| Task | Ghiotto | Rinaldi | Cossu | Ferrando | Oldani | Tessari | Maffeis | Fenoglio | Bertarelli | Supplier members |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Symptom description | A | C | R | R | I | I | C | I | I | I |
| Containment, stock and sorting | C | R | C | R | A, R | I | C | I | I | I |
| Laboratory analysis | C | C | A, R | I | I | I | C | I | I | C |
| Supplier process review | A, R | C | C | I | I | C | C | I | I | R |
| Replacement supply | C | I | I | C | C | A, R | C | I | I | R |
| Customer information | C | C | C | I | C | I | I | A, R | C | I |
| Overall plan and escalation | R | I | I | I | I | I | I | I | A | I |

### 1.5 Working rules of the team

#### 1.5.1 Meetings

- A short stand-up call of 15 minutes takes place every working day at 08:15 for the first two weeks. The call is held by Ghiotto. The attendees are Rinaldi, Cossu, Ferrando, Oldani and Tessari, and the supplier members join by video link.
- A longer team meeting of 90 minutes takes place every Thursday at 14:00.
- The sponsor receives a one-page summary from Ghiotto every Friday by 12:00.

#### 1.5.2 Information

All measurement data is entered into one shared workbook that is managed by Cossu. Each entry carries the date, the operator, the instrument and the clip or sample identity. Photographs are stored in one folder that is named by date. The supplier has read and write access to the supplier-process folder only, and read access to the measurement workbook.

#### 1.5.3 Decisions

The team decides by agreement among the members. If there is no agreement within one working day, Ghiotto brings the question to Bertarelli, who decides. Questions about stock use are decided by Rinaldi and Oldani together, because they know what has been measured and where the parts are.

#### 1.5.4 Time

The members have set time aside as follows.

| Member | Hours per week, weeks 1 and 2 | Hours per week afterwards |
|---|---|---|
| Ghiotto | 30 | 12 |
| Rinaldi | 36 | 10 |
| Cossu | 24 | 8 |
| Ferrando | 16 | 4 |
| Oldani | 20 | 4 |
| Tessari | 8 | 3 |
| Maffeis | 10 | 6 |
| Fenoglio | 6 | 2 |
| Zanetti | 6 | 0 |
| Marchesini | 8 | 4 |
| Bonomelli | 14 | 6 |
| Gervasoni | 12 | 4 |

### 1.6 Contact list and availability

The team uses a shared mailbox for the NCR. Each member also has a direct phone line. Outside normal hours, Ghiotto is reachable on his work mobile phone until 20:00 on working days. Ferrando covers the third shift for questions about the cells. The supplier members have given a direct line for the quality manager and a second for the production manager, and both can be reached from 07:00 to 17:30.

### 1.7 Limits of the team and external help

The team does not include an outside laboratory. If the Valsangone laboratory cannot give a result that the supplier accepts, for example for the microstructure, the team will agree on a third laboratory, and Cossu will prepare the samples. No such laboratory has been named at this time. A statistician from the Valsangone quality department, Gianluca Brambilla, is available for sampling plans and the analysis of the sorting data, and is invited to the Thursday meeting when needed. He is not a permanent member.

### 1.8 Training of the team on the clip

On 5 November, Maffeis gave a 40-minute briefing to members who do not work on the clip every day. She explained the function of the tab, the snap-in travel of about 2.4 mm, and why a hardness of more than 450 HV1 reduces the elastic range. She showed the cracked clips from the tray that Zanetti had saved. The supplier members could attend by video link, and Gervasoni asked for the photographs of the fracture surfaces, which were sent to him the same day.

## 3. D3 Containment details

## D3 Containment Details

### 3.1 Scope and aim

The aim of containment is to be sure that no clip with a hardness above 450 HV1 is used in production or sent to the customer, while the cause is still being found. It covers all CL-115 clips received from Minuterie Germanasca from 12 October 2026, in every form: loose clips, clips in line-side containers, clips with a sleeve in work in progress, and clips packed in kits. It also covers the 46,000 clips that were shipped before 3 November.

The quantity received was 186,000 clips in four deliveries. Of these, 140,000 clips were on site at 18:00 on 5 November 2026 and 46,000 had been shipped.

### 3.2 Stock locations and quantities

Oldani and two warehouse staff counted all locations on 4 and 5 November. The counts were made by pallet, bin and carton, and each count was checked by a second person.

| Location code | Place | Form of the clips | Quantity at 5 November, 18:00 | Marking before sorting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GR-Q | Goods receipt, quarantine area | Loose, fourth delivery, unopened | 30,000 | Red tag |
| W2 | Main warehouse, rack W2, levels 2 to 4 | Loose, remainder of deliveries 2 and 3 | 52,400 | Red tag |
| LS-B | Line-side containers, hall B | Loose, in kanban bins | 6,800 | Red tag |
| WIP-3 | Cell 3 and cell 1 buffer | Clips with sleeve, not yet in kits | 9,200 | Red tag |
| FG-4 | Finished goods warehouse, aisle 4 | Packed kits of 200 | 41,600 | Red tag |
| Total on site | | | 140,000 | |
| Shipped | In five shipments since 12 October | Packed kits | 46,000 | Customer informed |
| Total received | | | 186,000 | |

The quantities of the first delivery were mostly used before 3 November. This is why the first delivery makes up a small share of the stock on site and a large share of the shipped quantity.

### 3.3 Sorting plan

#### 3.3.1 Choice of method

A hardness measurement on each clip with an indenter would leave a mark and would take too long. The team chose a non-destructive eddy-current comparator that Rinaldi's group already uses for other spring parts. The device compares the electromagnetic response of each clip with that of reference clips. A harder clip gives a different signal from a softer one, so the device can separate the two.

The method was not used before on CL-115, so it was first proven. Cossu prepared 40 reference clips from the retained samples, each measured at HV1 on a section and then marked on the clip. He sorted them as follows.

| Reference group | Number of clips | Hardness range, HV1 | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: in limit, centre | 12 | 425 to 445 | Set the accept signal |
| B: in limit, near the upper edge | 8 | 446 to 450 | Set the accept limit |
| C: just above the limit | 10 | 452 to 470 | Test for the smallest detectable step |
| D: well above the limit | 10 | 485 to 540 | Set the reject signal |

The comparator limit was set at the signal level between groups B and C. The device then sorted all 40 reference clips correctly in three repeated runs. As the device had no error in these runs, the team added a safety margin: any clip within 5 per cent of the limit signal is also rejected. This gives up some good clips, and it reduces the risk that a bad clip is accepted.

#### 3.3.2 Checks during sorting

The comparator is checked with groups A and D at the start of every shift and after every 5,000 clips. If it misreads a reference clip, all clips sorted since the last good check are sorted again. Each shift also takes a sample of 50 accepted clips for a hardness measurement on sections by Cossu's laboratory. The sorting stops if one clip in a sample of 50 is above 450 HV1.

#### 3.3.3 Sorting steps by form

| Form | Method | Throughput | Staff | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Loose clips | Vibratory feeder into the comparator, automatic air-jet separation | about 2,400 clips per hour | 2 inspectors | Accept, reject and doubtful clips go to three bins |
| Clips with sleeve | Comparator with a larger probe, manual load | about 900 clips per hour | 3 inspectors | The polymer sleeve does not affect the signal, which was checked with 20 reference clips |
| Kits of 200 | Kits opened, clips and sleeves sorted separately, then repacked | about 600 clips per hour | 4 operators | Good sleeves are kept for reuse |

The doubtful bin takes all clips for which the signal is close to the limit. They are measured again, and if the second reading is also doubtful, they are treated as rejected.

### 3.4 Sorting results

Sorting began on 6 November and ended on 12 November 2026. Two shifts per day worked on the loose clips, and one shift on the other forms.

| Location | Quantity sorted | Accepted | Rejected | Reject share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GR-Q | 30,000 | 412 | 29,588 | 98.6 % |
| W2 | 52,400 | 9,860 | 42,540 | 81.2 % |
| LS-B | 6,800 | 1,950 | 4,850 | 71.3 % |
| WIP-3 | 9,200 | 2,300 | 6,900 | 75.0 % |
| FG-4 | 41,600 | 11,480 | 30,120 | 72.4 % |
| Total | 140,000 | 26,002 | 113,998 | 81.4 % |

The check samples of accepted clips, 50 per shift over 7 shifts, gave 350 hardness measurements. The highest was 449 HV1, and none was above the limit. Cossu also measured 100 clips that the comparator had rejected, and all of them were above 450 HV1. The lowest of these was 458 HV1.

The high reject share in the fourth delivery and in rack W2 is in line with the early data in D0, where the third and fourth deliveries were fully out of limit. The accepted clips come mostly from the first and second deliveries.

### 3.5 Handling of the rejected clips

Rejected clips were moved to a locked cage in the goods receipt area, labelled by origin, so that the later analysis can say which delivery they belong to. The total of 113,998 clips is kept as follows.

| Origin | Quantity | Storage | Remark |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loose clips, all locations | 77,978 | Cage R1, pallets 1 to 8 | Not to be used for any purpose |
| Clips from sleeve units | 6,900 | Cage R1, pallet 9 | Sleeves removed and kept |
| Clips from kits | 30,120 | Cage R1, pallets 10 to 14 | Cartons and sleeves recovered |

The three lines above give 114,998, which does not match the total. The correct total of loose clips is 76,978 (29,588 + 42,540 + 4,850), which gives 76,978 + 6,900 + 30,120 = 113,998. The cage list was corrected on 13 November, and the pallet counts were checked again.

A set of 600 rejected clips, with 150 from each delivery and from different pallets, was taken for the laboratory and the supplier. The rest of the rejected clips stay in the cage until a decision is made.

### 3.6 Clean-point marking

The clean point is the first piece of stock that is known to be in limit, and the marking shows this clearly on every pack. The marking has two parts: one for stock that was sorted at Valsangone and one for new supply from the supplier.

#### 3.6.1 Sorted stock at Valsangone

- Every accepted container, bin or carton gets a green label with the text SORTED 100 % and the sorting date, the shift, and the comparator check that was valid for that shift.
- A green-stamped dot is put on the carton corner and on the upper right of the kit label. A person can then see the mark from a distance of 3 m.
- Accepted stock goes to a separate location, W2-G, with the address W2-G-01 to W2-G-14. No other CL-115 stock may be placed in these locations.
- The ERP stock block was lifted only for the accepted quantity of 26,002 clips, and only when the physical green label was in place. The rejected quantity stays blocked.

#### 3.6.2 New supply from Minuterie Germanasca

The clean point for supplied clips is the first delivery for which the supplier has changed its tempering process and shows in-limit hardness results. Each carton of such a delivery must carry a blue band and the text 100 % VERIFIED on the label. The supplier will send hardness data from 5 pieces per furnace load with each delivery. Until this delivery arrives, Valsangone treats every new delivery as unsorted and measures a sample of 80 clips, with a full comparator sort if one clip is above the limit.

| Mark | Meaning | Where used |
|---|---|---|
| Red tag | Blocked, not sorted | All stock until sorting |
| Green label, SORTED 100 % | Sorted at Valsangone and accepted | W2-G, line-side, kits |
| Black label, REJECT | Sorted and rejected | Cage R1 |
| Blue band, 100 % VERIFIED | New supply with hardness data from the supplier | Next supplier deliveries |

### 3.7 Containment of kits made from accepted clips

When a kit is made with accepted clips, the sleeve-insertion cell records the lot of the accepted clips on the kit label. A kit built from accepted clips carries a green dot and the clean-point date. The first kit with the clean-point mark was packed on 9 November at 10:20 in cell 3. All operators in cell 3 and cell 1 received a short briefing from Ferrando on 6 November, with a sample of a cracked clip, so that they know what to do if cracking appears again. If one clip cracks, the operator stops the cell and informs the supervisor.

### 3.8 Shipped quantity

The shipped quantity of 46,000 clips cannot be sorted at Valsangone. The customer quality liaison sent Valsangone's shipment data to the customer on 4 November. Valsangone's records show that the five shipments were made on 14 October, 19 October, 22 October, 27 October and 30 October, with 9,000, 8,400, 10,600, 9,800 and 8,200 clips. The first two shipments were made mainly from the first delivery, whose hardness mean was 438 HV1 in the early sample. The last three were made from clips of the second and third deliveries. ## 4. Measurement results

### 1.1 Purpose and scope

The measurements cover six strip lots received between July and November 2026. They also cover the finished clips made from those lots and the checks carried out to confirm the measuring equipment was reliable.

### 1.2 Acceptance criteria used

The drawing requires a finished-clip hardness of 430 to 480 HV1, measured on a polished cross-section at mid-thickness. The material specification for the strip requires a tensile strength of 1,400 to 1,600 MPa. The strip thickness tolerance is 0.80 mm ± 0.03 mm. Where a measurement in this section is called out of range, it is measured against these limits only.

Samples were drawn per lot, from the head and tail of each coil and from the middle of the coil where the coil length allowed. Samples were mounted in a cold-setting resin, ground and polished before any hardness indentation, so that surface cold work from stamping could not influence the readings.

1. Three consecutive lots (3, 4, 5, total 16,200 kg) have strip and clip hardness 20 to 55 HV1 above the upper limit.
2. The condition is uniform along the coil and is not tied to a particular coil end.
3. Forming does not change the hardness meaningfully.
4. Thickness is in tolerance on all lots, and tensile strength is high in step with hardness.
5. Supplier certificate values disagree with Valsangone results on the affected lots only.

## 5. D4 Ishikawa analysis

### 2.1 Approach

The team built a cause-and-effect diagram around the problem statement: "CL-115 clips made from Germanasca C67S strip measure 487–538 HV1 against a limit of 430–480 HV1 and crack during installation." The team consisted of the quality engineer, the stamping process engineer, the incoming inspection lead, the laboratory technician and a purchasing representative. A metallurgist from the external laboratory and the Germanasca quality manager joined by video for the material and measurement branches. Each of the six branches below was assessed against the evidence in the measurement results. A cause was kept for further testing only when it could plausibly raise hardness uniformly across three consecutive lots.

**Table 5 – Summary of Ishikawa branches**

| Branch | Candidate causes raised | Carried to verification | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Man | 4 | 1 | Inspection reliance on certificate |
| Machine | 6 | 2 | Supplier tempering furnace control |
| Method | 5 | 2 | Supplier line speed and Valsangone acceptance method |
| Material | 5 | 1 | Carbon and alloy content check |
| Measurement | 5 | 1 | Supplier single-reading hardness check |
| Environment | 3 | 0 | No link to hardness |

### 2.2 Man

Four candidate causes were reviewed.

1. **Incoming inspector skipped a hardness check.** The inspection record shows that incoming inspection on strip covers thickness and width at each coil and does not include hardness. The inspector followed the instruction as written. This is not an individual error but it is a gap in what is asked of the person, and it explains why the problem reached the stamping line.
2. **Stamping operator mixed lots.** Lot traceability on the press shows no mixing. Lots 3, 4 and 5 were run in separate shifts with clear label records.
3. **Laboratory technician reading error.** Two technicians measured the same 10 mounts independently, and the results differed by a mean of 1.8 HV. This cannot account for a 45 HV shift.
4. **Supplier operator adjusted furnace settings.** The supplier operator log shows a line-speed increase on 15 September. This is carried to the Method branch.

The man branch therefore supports one point only: the people followed the written instructions, and the instructions did not ask for a hardness check on arrival.

### 2.3 Machine

Six causes were raised, covering both sites.

1. **Valsangone press or tooling work-hardening the strip.** Strip and clip hardness agree within 1.5 HV (Table 3), so tooling does not add hardness. Ruled out.
2. **Valsangone stamping force or speed.** Press settings were unchanged across all runs. Ruled out.
3. **Supplier tempering furnace temperature below setpoint.** The supplier's continuous tempering furnace has three zones controlled by one thermocouple each. Germanasca reported that the thermocouple in zone 3 was replaced on 10 September and checked against a handheld reference on 25 September, when it read 28 °C higher than the reference. A reading that is too high makes the controller supply less heat, so the strip is tempered cooler than intended. Carried to verification.
4. **Supplier quench cooling rate too high.** A faster quench would raise as-quenched hardness but tempering normally brings strip to a similar value. The supplier's quench data was unchanged. Considered unlikely.
5. **Supplier strip tension or leveller settings.** These affect flatness and not hardness. Ruled out.
6. **Supplier austenitising zone temperature.** Logged values stayed within ±5 °C. Carried to verification as a secondary check, together with the temper-time issue under Method.

### 2.4 Method

Five causes were reviewed.

1. **Supplier line speed increased.** The supplier raised line speed from 5.0 to 5.6 m/min on 15 September to meet a volume request. Soak time in the tempering zone fell from about 95 s to 85 s. Carried to verification.
2. **Supplier austenitising soak reduced.** The same speed increase reduced austenitising time. This affects grain size and carbide dissolution more than final hardness. Carried to verification through metallography.
3. **Valsangone acceptance method relies on the certificate.** The purchasing specification calls for a certificate with each lot and does not request a hardness check on arrival. This explains why the defect escaped, and it is carried forward with the Man branch.
4. **Valsangone storage method alters the strip.** Strip is stored at ambient temperature for less than 60 days. A temperature rise of this kind cannot change hardness. Ruled out.
5. **Clip forming sequence causes strain hardening.** Ruled out by Table 3.

### 2.5 Material

Five causes were reviewed.

1. **Carbon content above specification.** Higher carbon would raise the hardness after the same heat treatment. The specification range is 0.65 to 0.70 percent carbon. Spectrometer results for the three affected lots are reported in Section 3. Carried to verification.
2. **Alloy content such as manganese or silicon outside range.** Checked in the same spectrometer run.
3. **Wrong strip grade delivered.** The mill certificate and the spectrometer both show the correct grade family. Ruled out unless the spectrometer result contradicts it.
4. **Different steel mill source.** Germanasca confirmed that Lots 3 to 5 came from the same mill as Lots 1 and 2.
5. **Strip decarburised on the surface, lowering instead of raising hardness.** The direction is wrong for this defect. Ruled out.

### 2.6 Measurement

Five causes were reviewed.

1. **Valsangone tester reading high.** The reference block checks (Table 1) are within 1.2 HV, and the external laboratory's tester B gave results within 3.1 HV of tester A on 12 shared mounts. Ruled out.
2. **Specimen preparation raising hardness.** Mounts were cold-set and polished with light pressure. Surface layers were removed by at least 0.05 mm. Ruled out.
3. **Indentation too close to the edge.** Spacing was held above 2.5 diagonals from any edge. Ruled out.
4. **Conversion error between scales.** Hardness was read directly in HV, so no conversion was involved. Ruled out.
5. **Supplier measurement system.** The supplier certificate is based on one reading per coil, taken at the coil head with a portable tester. A single reading cannot show a drift of this size reliably, and the portable tester was last verified 14 months earlier. Carried to verification as a contributor to the escape.

### 2.7 Environment

Three causes were reviewed.

1. **Temperature of the laboratory.** The room was held between 20 °C and 23 °C. Hardness testers are insensitive to this range.
2. **Vibration near the tester.** The tester stands on an isolated bench. Reference blocks gave stable readings.
3. **Humidity or storage conditions at Valsangone.** Humidity affects surface rust, not through-thickness hardness. Ruled out.

The team found no environmental cause.

### 2.8 Conclusion of the Ishikawa review

The diagram points toward two production-side causes at the supplier, a tempering temperature below the intended value and a shorter soak time after a line-speed increase, and two detection-side causes, a one-reading supplier check and the lack of a hardness check at Valsangone incoming inspection. Chemistry stayed on the list until it could be checked in the laboratory. The remaining causes were set aside with evidence. Section 3 tests the retained causes.

## 6. D4 Five-why analysis and verification tests

### 3.1 Approach

The five-why analysis follows two chains. The first explains why the strip left the supplier too hard. The second explains why it was not detected before stamping. The laboratory tests that support each answer are described afterwards, so every answer in a chain can be traced to a measurement.

### 3.2 Why chain A – occurrence

**Problem:** Strip in Lots 3, 4 and 5 is 20 to 55 HV1 above the upper limit.

1. **Why was the strip too hard?** Because the martensite formed on quenching was tempered less than intended. The microstructure and re-temper tests in 3.6 and 3.7 show this.
2. **Why was it tempered less than intended?** Because the effective strip temperature in the tempering furnace was lower than the 420 °C setpoint, and the soak time was shorter than the validated 95 s.
3. **Why was the temperature lower and the time shorter?** The zone 3 thermocouple read 28 °C high after replacement, so the controller under-heated, and line speed was raised by 12 percent on 15 September.
4. **Why was the thermocouple error not detected, and why was line speed changed?** The replacement thermocouple was installed without a check against a reference, and the line-speed change was made as a scheduling decision without a heat-treatment review.
5. **Why was there no check or review?** The supplier's furnace procedure requires a reference check at the next monthly audit and not at replacement, and it does not list line speed as a controlled parameter for the tempering step.

**Root cause A:** The supplier's furnace control procedure allowed a thermocouple replacement and a line-speed increase without verifying the resulting tempering conditions.

### 3.3 Why chain B – escape

**Problem:** Out-of-range strip reached the stamping line and was formed into clips.

1. **Why did hard strip reach the stamping line?** Because incoming inspection did not measure hardness.
2. **Why did incoming inspection not measure hardness?** The inspection instruction for the strip lists thickness, width and surface only.
3. **Why does the instruction omit hardness?** When the material was first approved, the supplier had a clean record over 30 consecutive lots, and hardness was left to the certificate.
4. **Why was the certificate not questioned?** It showed values within range for every lot, and there was no comparison between certificate and plant data.
5. **Why was there no comparison?** The purchasing specification treated the certificate as sufficient evidence and had no periodic verification built in.

**Root cause B:** Valsangone's incoming inspection relied on a supplier certificate based on one reading per coil, with no independent hardness check.

### 3.4 Chemical composition check

The team had retained chemistry as a candidate. Samples from Lots 2, 3, 4 and 6 were analysed by optical emission spectrometry at the external laboratory, with three burns per sample.

**Table 6 – Chemical composition, mass percent (mean of three burns)**

| Element | Specification | Lot 2 | Lot 3 | Lot 4 | Lot 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Carbon | 0.65–0.70 | 0.67 | 0.68 | 0.67 | 0.68 |
| Manganese | 0.60–0.90 | 0.72 | 0.74 | 0.73 | 0.71 |
| Silicon | 0.15–0.35 | 0.24 | 0.25 | 0.24 | 0.23 |
| Phosphorus | max 0.025 | 0.012 | 0.013 | 0.012 | 0.011 |
| Sulphur | max 0.025 | 0.008 | 0.009 | 0.008 | 0.008 |

All lots are within the specification and the composition is equivalent between conforming and nonconforming lots. Chemistry is therefore not the cause.

### 3.5 Metallographic examination

Cross-sections of Lot 2 and Lot 4 strip were etched and examined at 500x and 1,000x.

**Table 7 – Metallography results**

| Feature | Lot 2 (conforming) | Lot 4 (nonconforming) |
|---|---|---|
| Matrix | Tempered martensite, uniform | Tempered martensite, finer carbide dispersion |
| Mean prior-austenite grain size (linear intercept) | 6.3 µm | 6.1 µm |
| Retained ferrite or bainite | None | None |
| Visible carbide size | 0.15–0.30 µm | 0.08–0.20 µm |
| Decarburised depth | 0.010 mm | 0.012 mm |
| Inclusions | Rated light | Rated light |

Grain size is the same, which supports the finding that austenitising was not the problem. The carbides in Lot 4 are smaller and more finely dispersed, which is a typical signature of tempering at a lower temperature or for a shorter time. Decarburisation is minor in both samples and well within the 0.020 mm allowance.

### 3.6 Furnace data review at the supplier

Germanasca supplied furnace logs for the production dates of Lots 2 to 6. For Lot 2, zone 3 showed an indicated 420 °C and a handheld reference of 419 °C. For Lots 3 to 5, zone 3 indicated 420 °C while the reference showed 392 °C. The shortfall of 28 °C matches the offset found on 25 September. With the shorter soak time, the supplier's heat-treatment engineer estimated the effective tempering condition to be equivalent to roughly 360 to 370 °C for 95 s. For Lot 6, the thermocouple had been replaced again and the reference read 418 °C.

### 3.7 Re-temper response test

To test whether the hard strip was simply under-tempered, coupons from Lot 2 and Lot 4 were re-tempered for 30 minutes in a laboratory furnace at several temperatures, then measured on Vickers tester A (n = 5 per condition).

**Table 8 – Re-temper response (mean HV1)**

| Condition | Lot 2 | Lot 4 |
|---|---|---|
| As received | 462 | 508 |
| 380 °C, 30 min | 461 | 504 |
| 400 °C, 30 min | 458 | 493 |
| 420 °C, 30 min | 452 | 477 |
| 440 °C, 30 min | 441 | 459 |
| 460 °C, 30 min | 427 | 440 |

Lot 4 softens steadily and approaches the Lot 2 curve as the temperature rises. The two lots respond in the same way, which confirms the same chemistry and base structure and supports under-tempering as the cause. A 420 °C re-temper brings Lot 4 inside the range, at 477 HV1, but the team did not use it as a rework route for this investigation.

### 3.8 Tensile and bend confirmation

Coupons re-tempered at 420 °C from Lot 4 gave a mean tensile strength of 1,578 MPa, inside the limit. Clips formed from re-tempered strip passed the 50-piece bend test with zero cracks in three repeats of 50, compared with 7 cracks in 50 for as-received Lot 4 clips.

### 3.9 Confirmation of root cause

The evidence from each test points in the same direction:

1. Chemistry is identical across conforming and nonconforming lots.
2. Grain size is identical, and carbides are finer in the hard lots.
3. The furnace reference check shows a 28 °C shortfall and a shorter soak time for the affected period.
4. Re-tempering hard strip returns it to the expected hardness and restores bend performance.
5. Lot 6, made after the thermocouple was corrected, measures 468.0 HV1 mean.

The reasons for the escape are also confirmed. Valsangone data differed from the certificate by 40 to 44 HV on the affected lots, and incoming inspection had no step that would have shown it.

## 7. D5 and D6 Candidate corrective actions

## 1.1 Basis for the options

- Three coils of C67S strip (0.60 mm x 32 mm, 2,610 kg in total) came from Minuterie Germanasca and were received on 22 September 2026.
- The hardness specification for the strip is 430 to 470 HV1. Measured values on the three coils were 488 to 521 HV1, with a mean of 503 HV1.
- Clips formed from these coils cracked at the snap leg. The crack rate in customer assembly tests was 0.8 percent, against a normal level below 30 ppm.
- The D4 analysis found that the control thermocouple in tempering zone 3 of the supplier's furnace read about 22 °C higher than the true strip temperature. The strip was under-tempered and came out too hard.
- Two escape causes sit on our side. Incoming inspection relied on the mill certificate, and the in-house limit for finished clips was 440 to 500 HV1, which is wider than the strip specification.

The options therefore had to address three things: the supplier's furnace control, our detection at receiving, and our detection in process.

## 1.2 Options considered

Seven candidate actions were listed in the team meeting of 9 November 2026. Each was scored from 1 (poor) to 5 (best) against five criteria. The weights are effectiveness 35, detectability 25, speed 15, cost 15 and supply risk 10. The weighted score is the sum of weight times score, divided by 100.

| Option | Description | Effect. (35) | Detect. (25) | Speed (15) | Cost (15) | Supply (10) | Weighted score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Hardness test on every incoming coil at head, middle and tail | 3 | 5 | 5 | 4 | 4 | 4.05 |
| B | Supplier furnace measures: thermocouple replacement, second control thermocouple, data logger, hardness test on every coil | 5 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3.85 |
| C | Tighten the finished-clip hardness limit to 435 to 465 HV1 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 4 | 3.95 |
| D | Qualify a second strip source | 4 | 3 | 1 | 2 | 5 | 3.10 |
| E | Force-signature monitoring on the forming press to detect brittle parts | 3 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 4 | 3.05 |
| F | Re-temper the retained hard stock in our oven | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 5 | 2.60 |
| G | Change to a thicker section or a different steel grade | 4 | 3 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2.65 |

Option G was dropped. It would change the clip stiffness and the fit in the customer's harness clip, and the redesign effort is out of proportion to a furnace control fault. Option F scores low as a permanent fix because it treats the symptom. It is still worth testing, because it might recover part of the retained stock.

## 1.3 Candidate corrective actions selected for trial

The team chose a layered approach. Options A, B and C form the permanent set. Options D and E are run as parallel trials because they reduce the supply and detection risk over the longer term. Option F is tested only as a way to deal with the retained stock.

- **Option A** fixes the detection gap at receiving. It is quick and independent of the supplier.
- **Option B** removes the cause at its source. It depends on the supplier's cooperation, so Marco Bellandi will join the supplier's visit.
- **Option C** closes the gap that let hard clips pass in our own process.
- **Option D** protects supply if the supplier cannot hold the hardness window.
- **Option E** gives a second detection layer, but only if the trial shows it separates hard clips from normal ones.

## 8. D7 Preventive actions and lessons learned

## 2.1 Scope of the preventive work

D7 asks what else could fail in the same way, and what must change so that this class of failure is caught early on any part and any line. The D4 analysis showed a failure chain with three links: a supplier process drift, an incoming check that relied on paper, and a finished-part limit that was too wide. The preventive actions address each link for all products that use hardened and tempered strip, not only the CL-115 clip.

The actions below are planned. Owners and dates are shown so that progress can be tracked in the monthly quality meeting.

## 2.2 Process FMEA updates planned

The process FMEA for the CL-115 forming line will be revised in the week of 7 December 2026. Five rows are added or re-rated. The ratings are severity (S), occurrence (O) and detection (D) on a 1 to 10 scale. The "after" ratings are the values expected once the actions in D6 are in place, and they will be checked against trial data before they are entered.

| No. | Process step | Failure mode | Cause | S | O | D | RPN before | O after | D after | RPN after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Receiving of strip | Hardness above range not detected | Reliance on mill certificate, no hardness test | 8 | 5 | 7 | 280 | 3 | 3 | 72 |
| 2 | Supplier tempering | Strip under-tempered | Control thermocouple drift, no redundancy | 8 | 4 | 6 | 192 | 2 | 3 | 48 |
| 3 | Finished-clip hardness check | Hard clips pass | Limit of 440 to 500 HV1 wider than strip specification | 8 | 4 | 6 | 192 | 4 | 3 | 96 |
| 4 | Forming | Crack at snap leg not noticed | No force-signature monitoring, visual check only | 8 | 3 | 6 | 144 | 3 | 3 | 72 |
| 5 | Coil to lot traceability | Affected clips not found quickly | Coil number not on every container label | 6 | 3 | 5 | 90 | 2 | 3 | 36 |
| | **Total** | | | | | | **898** | | | **324** |

The expected total reduction is 64 percent. Row 3 stays the highest after-action value because the tighter limit lowers the chance of passing a hard clip only by detection, not by occurrence. Row 4 depends on Trial 5. If the monitor does not meet its criteria, the D rating for that row stays at 6 and the RPN stays at 144.

## 2.3 Control plan updates planned

The control plan will be updated by Davide Cattaneo and Giulia Ferrante at the same time as the FMEA. The planned changes are:

| Characteristic | Method | Sample size | Frequency | Limit | Reaction | Owner | Target date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strip hardness | Vickers HV1 in laboratory | 3 positions per coil (head, middle, tail) | Every coil | 430 to 470 HV1; range in coil no more than 25 HV | Hold coil, inform Supplier Quality, retest at 6 extra points | Marco Bellandi | 30 Nov 2026 |
| Strip hardness trend | Chart of coil means by supplier | All coils | Weekly review | Mean within 440 to 460 HV1 | Call to supplier if 3 points drift in one direction | Giulia Ferrante | 11 Jan 2027 |
| Finished-clip hardness | Vickers HV1 | 5 clips | Every 2 hours | 435 to 465 HV1 | Stop line, sort back to last good check | Davide Cattaneo | 25 Jan 2027 |
| Snap-leg flex test | Manual flex to 90 degrees, 3 cycles | 10 clips | Start of shift and after each coil change | No cracks | Stop line, hold lot | Elena Rinaldi | 11 Jan 2027 |
| Coil number on container label | Visual check at packing | Every container | Every container | Coil number legible and matches the traveller | Re-label before storage | Elena Rinaldi | 4 Jan 2027 |
| Forming force signature | Load cell on press | 100 percent | Continuous | Within band set in Trial 5 | Reject part, alarm after 5 in a row | Paolo Vitale | 15 Mar 2027 |

## 2.4 Other lines checked

From 9 to 13 November 2026, Quality checked every line that processes hardened and tempered strip. The check was a hardness test at head, middle and tail on every coil in stock or on the machine at that time, using the method from Trial 1. The results are below.

| Line | Product family | Strip grade and source | Coils checked | Readings | Range (HV1) | Remark |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Line 4 | Narrow cable clips | C67S, Minuterie Germanasca | 5 | 15 | 441 to 468 | All in range |
| Line 6 | Retaining spring clips | C67S, Minuterie Germanasca | 4 | 12 | 447 to 474 | One coil with edge readings 472 and 474; six extra points 458 to 471, mean 465 |
| Line 7 | Panel clips | C67S, other supplier | 3 | 9 | 436 to 459 | All in range |
| Line 9 | Terminal springs | Lower-carbon spring steel, other supplier | 2 | 6 | 381 to 396 | In range for that specification |
| Line 11 | Hose clamp bands | Lower-carbon spring steel, other supplier | 3 | 9 | 372 to 401 | In range for that specification |

The check covered 17 coils and 51 readings. The only reading outside the range on a line using the same supplier was the pair at Line 6. The coil mean was inside the range, but the supplier's tail section could be drifting. Marco Bellandi has raised this with Franco Bertola and added the coil to the weekly trend chart. Lines 4 and 6 will have their next 6 coils tested at 5 positions instead of 3.

## 2.5 Horizontal deployment to other suppliers

The same weakness, reliance on a certificate without a measurement, was found at receiving for two other strip suppliers. The plan is:

1. Extend the three-position hardness test to all hardened strip suppliers by 30 November 2026.
2. Ask each supplier for a recent furnace calibration record by 18 December 2026.
3. Add furnace thermocouple replacement intervals to the supplier questionnaire from the next audit cycle. The first audit under the new questionnaire is the one at Minuterie Germanasca on 7 December 2026.

## 2.6 Training

Twenty people will be trained between 30 November and 18 December 2026: 6 receiving staff, 14 press and packing operators. Content covers how hardness relates to crack risk in spring steel, how to read the new charts, and the reaction plan. Sofia Marchetti will organise a one-hour session for buyers on why certificates are not a substitute for measurement on safety-relevant spring parts.

## 2.7 Lessons learned

| No. | Lesson | Evidence | Action or deployment | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A certificate shows what the supplier intended, not what the strip is | Mill certificate showed 452 HV1 average, our test showed 503 HV1 | Measure every coil at receiving | Marco Bellandi |
| 2 | Internal limits must not be wider than the specification | Finished-clip limit of 440 to 500 HV1 against strip specification of 430 to 470 HV1 | Review all limits against specifications on the five highest-volume products by 29 Jan 2027 | Giulia Ferrante |
| 3 | A single thermocouple is a single point of failure | Zone 3 reading 22 °C off the true value | Ask for redundancy or calibration evidence at audits | Marco Bellandi |
| 4 | Traceability speed decides the cost of containment | Two days to find all clips from the three coils | Coil number on every label | Elena Rinaldi |
| 5 | Hardness failures appear late | Cracks first showed in customer assembly | Flex test at start of shift and after coil change | Elena Rinaldi |

## 2.8 Indicators for preventive actions

The following indicators will be reviewed monthly from January 2027.

| Indicator | Target | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Coils tested at receiving | 100 percent | Receiving log |
| Coils with any reading outside range | Below 2 percent | Laboratory data |
| Finished-clip hardness readings outside 435 to 465 HV1 | Below 1 percent | Line charts |
| Cracks at snap leg found in customer assembly | Below 30 ppm | Customer feedback |
| Supplier furnace log files received on time | 100 percent | Supplier Quality |

## 9. Cost of poor quality

## 3.1 Scope and basis

This section records the cost of poor quality linked to the hard CL-115 clips, from receipt of the strip on 22 September 2026 to 13 November 2026. All amounts are in euros and exclude VAT. Hourly rates are the plant's standard internal rates for 2026. Time was taken from booked hours on the containment jobs and from the engineering time sheets. External costs are from invoices received to date. The forecast cost of the corrective action trials in D5 and D6 (€12,750) is not included in the total below, because it is spending on improvement and not a loss from the defect.

## 3.2 Quantities involved

| Item | Quantity |
|---|---|
| Strip coils affected | 3 coils, 2,610 kg |
| Clips formed from these coils | 1,030,000 pieces |
| Clips already shipped to the customer | 196,000 pieces |
| Clips held at Valsangone (stock and work in progress) | 834,000 pieces |
| Held clips that passed the sort | 558,000 pieces |
| Held clips scrapped | 276,000 pieces (33.1 percent of held clips) |
| Strip not yet formed, scrapped | 480 kg |

The 276,000 scrapped clips include 14,900 clips returned after sorting at the customer's line. The sale value of the lot at the standard price of €0.062 per clip is €63,860.

## 3.3 Sorting hours

Containment took 540 sorting hours over 19 working days. Six operators worked in three shifts, supported by a rented eddy-current sorter. The hours are split as follows.

| Activity | Hours | Remark |
|---|---|---|
| Eddy-current sorting of held clips | 212 | Throughput about 3,900 clips per hour including set-up and calibration with reference clips |
| Manual flex check on clips the sorter flagged as doubtful | 188 | About 38,000 clips checked |
| Re-boxing and re-labelling of sorted lots | 74 | Includes lot splitting by coil |
| Counting, traceability records and scrap tagging | 66 | Includes reconciliation with press records |
| **Total** | **540** | |

Of the total, 118 hours were worked as overtime on Saturdays and in the evening to protect delivery dates. The overtime premium is shown as a separate line below. The hours in the table are charged at the standard rate, and the premium is charged only on the 118 overtime hours.

## 3.4 Cost table

| No. | Cost item | Quantity | Unit rate (€) | Amount (€) | Category |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sorting labour at Valsangone | 540 h | 36.00 | 19,440 | Appraisal and containment |
| 2 | Overtime premium | 118 h | 18.00 | 2,124 | Appraisal and containment |
| 3 | Rental of eddy-current sorter, 3 weeks | 1 | 4,200.00 | 4,200 | Appraisal and containment |
| 4 | External laboratory hardness tests | 96 samples | 38.00 | 3,648 | Appraisal and containment |
| 5 | Internal laboratory time | 64 h | 42.00 | 2,688 | Appraisal and containment |
| | **Subtotal appraisal and containment** | | | **32,100** | |
| 6 | Scrapped clips | 276,000 pcs | 0.0185 | 5,106 | Internal failure |
| 7 | Scrapped strip | 480 kg | 3.10 | 1,488 | Internal failure |
| 8 | Press downtime for coil changes and re-setup | 22 h | 145.00 | 3,190 | Internal failure |
| 9 | Engineering and quality time | 210 h | 58.00 | 12,180 | Internal failure |
| | **Subtotal internal failure** | | | **21,964** | |
| 10 | Express road freight for replacement strip | 1 | 1,350.00 | 1,350 | External failure |
| 11 | Premium road freight of sorted clips | 2 shipments | 1,430.00 | 2,860 | External failure |
| 12 | Air freight of one pallet of sorted clips | 1 | 3,940.00 | 3,940 | External failure |
| 13 | Sorting at the customer's line | 160 h | 32.00 | 5,120 | External failure |
| | **Subtotal external failure** | | | **13,270** | |
| | **Total cost of poor quality** | | | **67,334** | |

The unit cost of €0.0185 per scrapped clip is the average cost accumulated at the point of scrap: strip, forming and handling. The average clip weighs 1.9 g, so the strip content alone is about €0.0059.

## 3.5 Distribution by category

| Category | Amount (€) | Share of total |
|---|---|---|
| Appraisal and containment | 32,100 | 47.7 percent |
| Internal failure | 21,964 | 32.6 percent |
| External failure | 13,270 | 19.7 percent |
| **Total** | **67,334** | **100.0 percent** |

Almost half of the cost is the effort to find out which clips were good. This follows from the fact that hardness cannot be seen on the clip, so the whole held quantity had to be sorted by instrument. Engineering and quality time (€12,180) is the largest single line after sorting labour, because the investigation involved the supplier, the laboratory and three production lines.

## 3.6 Freight detail

There were four freight movements.

1. **Replacement strip.** One express road delivery of 900 kg of strip from the supplier on 29 September, at €1,350, so that the press could keep running while the three coils were blocked.
2. **Two premium road shipments.** Each carried 41,000 sorted clips to the customer's plant, at €1,430 each, in place of the normal weekly shipment on economy rates.
3. **One air freight pallet.** The pallet carried 38,000 clips to cover a stock-out on the customer's line, at €3,940.
4. **Customer sorting.** The customer sorted the 196,000 shipped clips on its line over 160 hours, at €32.00 per hour, as charged to us.

The extra freight cost, compared with normal economy shipments, was about 86 percent of the invoiced freight. The normal cost for the same quantities would have been about €1,490 for the sorted clip shipments, so the avoidable part of the freight is €5,310 of the €8,150 in lines 10 to 12.

## 3.7 Scrap detail

Scrap came from three sources.

| Source | Quantity | Amount (€) |
|---|---|---|
| Clips rejected by eddy-current sort at Valsangone | 261,100 pcs | 4,830 |
| Clips returned after sorting at the customer | 14,900 pcs | 276 |
| Strip not yet formed | 480 kg | 1,488 |
| **Total** | | **6,594** |

The first two rows add to 276,000 clips and €5,106. The scrap is a small part of the total, because the clips are low-value parts. The cost of finding them was much higher than their value.

## 3.8 Items not included in the total

The following are not counted, so the total is a lower bound:

- Possible recovery from Minuterie Germanasca, which is a commercial matter and is not offset against the loss here.
- Management time for customer meetings and the supplier visit on 7 December 2026.
- Cost of the lost production slots on the press, beyond the 22 hours of downtime.
- Forecast cost of the corrective action trials (€12,750).

## 3.9 Ratios

| Ratio | Value |
|---|---|
| Cost of poor quality as a share of sale value of the lot (€63,860) | 105.4 percent |
| Cost per clip formed from the three coils (1,030,000 pieces) | €0.0654 |
| Sorting hours per 1,000 clips held (834,000 pieces) | 0.65 h |
| Cost per kg of affected strip (2,610 kg) | €25.80 |

The cost of the event is larger than the revenue of the affected lot. A single hardness test of three coils, at about €38 per sample, would have cost less than €350 and would have found the problem on the day of receipt. Giulia Ferrante will update this section if any further invoices arrive.

## Supplier history

NCR-25-088, Minuterie Germanasca (SUP-G): CL-115 hardness at the upper limit in 2025. Status: closed after retraining of the heat treatment operators. A similar issue on HS-410 heat shields (DC04) at another supplier is unrelated.
